name: South Route
approach: Start at the Pete Lake Trailhead (~2,840 ft) at the end of Cooper Lake Road (Forest Road 46) off the Salmon La Sac Road. Follow the Pete Lake Trail (#1323) roughly 4.5 miles of gentle, mostly flat forest walking along the Cooper River to Pete Lake. From Pete Lake, continue up the Lemah Creek/Lemah Meadows drainage (watch for windfall and thick vine maple in the meadow bypass) to join the Pacific Crest Trail; turn right (north) and climb the PCT's long switchback section roughly 4-4.5 more miles to Lower and Upper Vista Lake (~5,500-5,600 ft) — camp is commonly made here, making this a two-day approach of about 10 miles and 2,800 ft to reach the alpine basin. This is also the last reliable water before the high basin — carry extra, as the route above is reported bone-dry until you're back near Vista Lakes. From Vista Lakes, leave the PCT and traverse cross-country north along Vista Ridge toward Summit Chief Pass, crossing a convoluted series of sandstone/siltstone slabs cut by numerous slots and gullies; stay left (west) of Summit Chief Lake and minimize elevation loss while rounding into the southeast basin below the peak. Many parties stash overnight gear around 6,300 ft in the lower talus basin before the final push. From there, traverse steep hardpan and talus (rockfall potential from parties above) up to a notch near 7,200 ft, then work into the southwest gully system — loose rock and an exposed, slightly outward-dipping slab lead through the final Class 2-3 scrambling to the summit. Route-finding through the upper basin and the southwest gully is the crux of the approach; online photos of the south-ridge crossing point are frequently reported as inaccurate, so err toward careful navigation rather than trusting a single beta photo. The route's real crux is often a moat around 7,000 ft where the peak steepens; it can become impassable after mid-July, sometimes earlier in a low-snow year.
descent: This is a walk-off/downclimb — no rappelling is involved on the standard South Route. Reverse the ascent line exactly: downclimb the loose, exposed southwest gully and its outward-dipping slab back to the ~7,200 ft notch, taking care with the loose rock and steep dirt in the upper 500 feet (this section has real rockfall potential for parties below). Continue down through the talus and hardpan to the 6,300 ft basin (recover any stashed gear here), then retrace the slab traverses back onto Vista Ridge and down to Vista Lakes/the PCT. From Vista Lakes, follow the PCT switchbacks back down to Lemah Meadows and the Pete Lake Trail, then out to the Pete Lake Trailhead. Some parties vary the return by continuing along the PCT to Waptus Lake and crossing Waptus Pass back to the Pete Lake trailhead as an alternate loop. The round trip runs roughly 25 miles car to car, so most parties treat this as an overnight with a basin or Vista Lakes camp rather than a single push.
hazards: Moat crux near 7,000 ft — can be impassable after mid-July, sometimes earlier in low-snow years
Loose, rotten sandstone/siltstone rock across the traversing slabs and especially the upper 500 ft below the summit
Route-finding: several similar-looking snow fingers lead toward the south ridge but only one reaches the correct notch — the wrong one can cliff out
Steep, often icy morning gully just past the ridge notch
Long, remote approach with stream crossings and limited bail options once committed to the face

waysIn.name: Pete Lake and the PCT switchbacks to the Vista Lakes tarns
waysIn.season: Roughly Jul-Sep, but see the moat note — the gate at 7,000 ft can shut by mid-July, earlier in a thin snow year
waysIn.notes:
Walk the Pete Lake trail #1323 up the Cooper River to a fork at about 3,120 ft, roughly five miles in. Turn right, continue about six tenths of a mile, and turn right again onto the Pacific Crest Trail at about 3,220 ft. Follow the PCT four and a half miles up a long series of switchbacks to about 5,500 ft.

The Vista Lakes tarns lie east of the trail at that height and hold the good bivy sites. Summit Chief is about two more miles from there. Reported times from the car to the upper lake run to most of a day with overnight loads, and every published account treats this as a two- or three-day trip.

This is also the last reliable water. The ground above is reported bone dry until you come back down to the lakes.

From camp, leave the PCT and traverse cross-country toward Summit Chief Pass, then follow the ridge north-west staying below the cliffs and gendarmes, into the upper basin south-east of the main summit. One party's hindsight on this traverse is worth having: they should have dropped to about 6,000 ft and taken the scree instead of holding height across steep sloping slabs.
hazards: A moat around 7,000 ft that can close the route outright after mid-July
Icy gully beyond the notch in the morning — crampons are worth carrying for it
Steep dirt and very loose rock on the final five hundred feet
Rockfall from parties above on the hardpan and talus below the notch
No water at all above the Vista Lakes
Sloping slabs on the traverse from camp, avoidable by dropping to the scree around 6,000 ft

waysIn.name: Lemah Meadow shortcut, cutting the PCT switchbacks
waysIn.season: Same window; the bypass is brushier and is a trade of distance for thrashing
waysIn.notes: A recorded variant that saves about three miles. After gaining roughly a thousand feet on the tight PCT switchbacks, leave the trail at the corner around 4,000 ft and head north, climbing about six hundred feet to the crest. The party who did it found plenty of windfall and pockets of vine maple, and called it irritating rather than difficult. It is a single-source variant, so treat the line as a hint rather than a route.
hazards: Windfall and vine maple on the bypass
No tread and no cairns
Same moat and loose-rock hazards above
waysIn.whyThisWay: To trade a few miles of switchbacks for a brushy, windfall-strewn cut across the hillside; for parties who would rather thrash than walk the longer trail.

name: East Slopes (Standard)
approach: Drive Hwy 101 to just before Sequim Bay State Park, turn onto Louella Rd, then Palo Alto Rd (becomes FR 28) for about 6 miles, turn right on FR 2880 along the Dungeness River, then in 1.7 miles turn left on FR 2870 and continue roughly 6.5–9 miles (gravel, winds steeply down to a river crossing) to the large Dungeness/Royal Basin trailhead lot (picnic table, vault toilet). Hike the Royal Basin Trail 7.2 miles / 2,500 ft gain to Royal Lake (~5,100 ft), then continue about 1 more mile / 500 ft gain into Upper Royal Basin (~5,600–5,700 ft) below The Needles. From there it's off-trail talus and a gully scramble to Sundial's summit ridge. From Upper Royal Basin, aim for the northeast-facing gully/couloir on climber's right of The Needles group (holds snow into July — axe/crampons helpful); the gully doglegs left below a notch on the summit ridge, then a short, exposed Class 3 scramble leads south to the true summit.
descent: Reverse the northeast couloir and East Face scramble back through Upper Royal Basin to camp at Royal Lake, then retrace the Royal Basin Trail out to the Upper Dungeness Trailhead — this route involves no glacier travel and is unrelated to the Hoh River/Mount Olympus approach.
hazards: Loose, rotten Eocene basalt typical of the Olympics — rockfall risk to yourself and any party below on the gully/ridge
Snow-filled or sluffing NE couloir well into July, requiring an ice axe and good self-arrest skills
Exposed Class 3 ridge traverse to the true summit
Unbridged creek crossings and a footlog on the Royal Basin approach
Remoteness — The Needles are lightly visited, so a rescue would take considerably longer than on popular Cascade peaks

waysIn.name: Royal Basin to the northeast gully
waysIn.season: Mid-July to September
waysIn.notes: Seven miles or so up the Royal Basin Trail to Royal Lake, then about a mile more and five hundred feet past Shelter Rock and through Arrowhead Meadow into Upper Royal Basin below the Needles. It has no designated sites (camping there is on bare ground or gravel only, by a permit arranged through the Wilderness Information Center), so most parties camp at the lake; the tarns are the last dependable water before the talus. Off-trail from the basin onward.
hazards: Loose, rotten basalt on the gully and ridge with rockfall onto parties below
Snow or sluffing in the northeast couloir well into July — axe and self-arrest
An exposed Class 3 ridge traverse to the true summit
A spot on the ledges that appears to cliff out and is passed by a cairned crack
Lightly visited terrain where a rescue takes considerably longer than usual

name: Standard Route (Southwest Face)
approach: Drive WA-20 (North Cascades Highway) to the Ross Dam Trailhead (MP 134). Descend about 1 mile on the Ross Dam trail/service road to Ross Lake, then cross via the Ross Lake Resort water taxi (on-demand, ~$4-5/person) or by hiking/paddling around, and pick up the Big Beaver Trail north along the lake. Follow it roughly 10 miles to Luna Camp, then continue about 1.5 miles further to the Access Creek drainage; leave the trail and climb the brushy, moderately steep Access Creek valley (staying on its north side is recommended) to the open basin east of Luna Peak (~4,300 ft) — described as the easiest, least-brushy approach on the east side of the Pickets. From there, climb to Access Col, cross to Luna Col, and traverse cross-country and glaciated terrain over Luna Peak, East Fury and West Fury to reach the Swiss–Fury saddle. An alternate southern approach reaches Swiss via Bacon Creek Road, Porkbelly Ridge, Mystery Ridge, Jasper Pass, Pioneer Ridge and Mt. Crowder's NE ridge down to a camp at Pickell Pass, from which Swiss's south side is climbed directly.
descent: There is no independent 'summit and go home' descent — retreat means reversing whichever approach line was used. From the summit, downclimb near the northwest ridge back toward the saddle with West Fury, re-cross the glacier/snowfield, and either return to a West Fury camp or continue the high traverse. Parties on the southern line downclimb the class 3 south side directly back to the Pickell Pass heather bench camp. Either way, exiting the range afterward requires committing to one of the long approach drainages (Access Creek to Big Beaver Trail/Ross Lake in the north, or Easy Ridge/Chilliwack/Hannegan Pass and Bacon Creek in the south) — both are multi-mile, partly off-trail hikes back to a trailhead.
hazards: Small glacier/permanent snowfield crossing northwest of West Fury en route to the Swiss-Fury saddle carries crevasse and moat hazard.
Extreme remoteness — any injury or major weather event requires multi-day self-rescue; this is not a location with quick helicopter-accessible bailout.
Approach drainages (Access Creek, Porkbelly Ridge, Mystery Ridge) involve steep, brushy, sometimes cliffy off-trail travel with route-finding hazard independent of the peak itself.

waysIn.name: The northern line: Access Creek and Luna Col, then the high traverse over Luna, East Fury and West Fury to the Swiss-Fury saddle
waysIn.season: Jul-Sep
waysIn.notes:
From the Ross Dam Trailhead at milepost 134 on WA-20, about a mile of trail and service road drops to Ross Lake, crossed by the resort water taxi or by paddling or walking round. Pick up the Big Beaver Trail north along the lake and follow it roughly 10 miles to Luna Camp, then about 1.5 miles further to the Access Creek drainage.

Leave the trail and climb the brushy, moderately steep Access Creek valley, staying on its north side, to the open basin east of Luna Peak at about 4,300 ft. This is described as the easiest and least brushy approach on the east side of the Pickets. From there, gain Access Col and traverse cross-country and glaciated terrain over Luna Peak, East Fury and West Fury to reach the Swiss-Fury saddle.
hazards: Glacier or snowfield crossing near West Fury toward the saddle carries crevasse and moat hazard
Traverse over Luna, East Fury and West Fury is required just to reach the saddle
Steep brushy off-trail travel in the Access Creek drainage
Extreme remoteness, no quick bailout; any injury means multi-day self-rescue
Exposed knife-edge summit ridge with a roughly 2,000 ft drop into Luna Cirque
Loose rock on some approach pinnacles

waysIn.name: The southern line: Bacon Creek Road, Porkbelly and Mystery Ridges, Jasper Pass and Crowder's northeast ridge to Pickell Pass
waysIn.season: Jul-Sep
waysIn.notes:
The alternate, and the shorter of the two in spirit if not in effort. It reaches Swiss from the south via Bacon Creek Road, Porkbelly Ridge, Mystery Ridge, Jasper Pass, Pioneer Ridge and Mount Crowder's northeast ridge, down to a camp at Pickell Pass.

This line is off-trail for most of its length, so treat the ridge sequence as the route rather than any particular tread.
hazards: Long off-trail ridge sequence over Porkbelly, Mystery and Pioneer ridges and Crowder's northeast ridge with no tread
Steep, brushy, sometimes cliffy off-trail terrain
No independent descent; leaving the range means a long off-trail drainage exit
Class 3 south side above Pickell Pass, downclimbed on return
Exposed knife-edge summit ridge with a roughly 2,000 ft drop into Luna Cirque
Extreme remoteness, any injury means multi-day self-rescue
waysIn.whyThisWay: For parties starting from the Bacon Creek road side who want to skip the Ross Lake crossing and Big Beaver trail, accepting a long, pathless ridge route with no tread to follow.

name: Table Mountain Trail (Standard)
approach: From the Artist Point trailhead (elev. ~5,100 ft, at the end of Mt. Baker Highway/SR 542, GPS approx. 48.847, -121.693) walk to the northwest corner of the large paved parking lot — the signed Table Mountain Trail #681 starts opposite the vault toilets, on the side of the lot away from the highway. The trail begins as a rock-lined gravel path that climbs gently before reaching its first switchback within a few hundred feet. From there the route ascends a tight set of rocky switchbacks blasted directly into the cliff band on Table Mountain's southeast face — this is the crux of the approach: a narrow, exposed catwalk with steep drop-offs toward the Chain Lakes basin and Swift Creek drainage 400-800 ft below. Footing here is loose rock and gravel over hard-packed tread, and snow or verglas frequently lingers in this cliff section into July, making it the most hazardous stretch of the whole route; many parties turn back here in early season without traction devices. After roughly 400 ft of gain (about 0.4-0.5 mi from the car) the switchbacks top out on the broad, relatively flat summit plateau ("the table"). From here follow the well-trodden tread west/northwest along the south rim, which gives open views straight down onto the Chain Lakes Trail; numerous braided use-trails cross the plateau but the main route hugs the south side. At about 1.2 mi you reach the east side of the tabletop with views of Mount Baker and Ptarmigan Ridge, and by 1.3 mi you arrive at two small tarns that frame Mount Shuksan — a natural turnaround for most day hikers and the last easily identified landmark before the trail degrades into a sketchy, unmaintained scramble path descending toward the Table Mountain Glacier. There is no reliable water along the route: the summit tarns are shallow, silty, and not worth treating, so carry all water from the car. Overall to the high point is roughly 1.4-1.5 mi one-way with about 700-725 ft of gain from the trailhead.
descent: Descend by reversing the ascent route — this is a walk-off, out-and-back trail with no rappelling required. From the tarns/plateau area, follow the south-rim tread back east across the tabletop to the head of the switchbacks, then downclimb the same cliff-band switchback trail carved into the southeast face back to the Artist Point parking lot. The switchback section demands the same care going down as coming up (often more, since loose gravel and any residual snow/ice patches are more consequential underfoot on descent, and the exposure is more psychologically apparent facing downhill); microspikes or trekking poles are worth carrying if snow lingers, which is common through early-to-mid summer. Stay on the established tread rather than cutting switchbacks — the rock is loose and the slope drops steeply toward Chain Lakes. No stream crossings or route-finding hazards on the way down beyond staying on the main trail through the braided plateau paths. Total descent is a mirror of the approach: about 1.4-1.5 mi and 700-725 ft back to the car.
hazards: Exposed cliff-face switchbacks with loose gravel/scree
Lingering snow and ice on the switchbacks into early summer
Cornices on the plateau's north rim above the Table Mountain Glacier remnant
No cell service at the trailhead or on the mountain

waysIn.name: Table Mountain Trail #681 from the Artist Point lot, up the southeast-face switchbacks
waysIn.season: Roughly Jul-Sep, and it is the road and the snow in the cliff band that decide it rather than the calendar
waysIn.notes:
From the Artist Point trailhead at about 5,100 ft, at the end of the Mount Baker Highway, walk to the northwest corner of the large paved parking lot. Table Mountain Trail #681 starts opposite the vault toilets, on the side of the lot away from the highway.

The trail begins as a rock-lined gravel path and reaches its first switchback within a few hundred feet. From there it climbs a tight set of rocky switchbacks blasted directly into the cliff band on Table Mountain's southeast face — a narrow, exposed catwalk with drops of 400-800 ft toward the Chain Lakes basin and Swift Creek.

After roughly 400 ft of gain, about 0.4-0.5 mile from the car, the switchbacks top out on the broad flat summit plateau. Follow the tread west-northwest along the south rim; braided use-trails cross the plateau but the main route hugs the south side. At about 1.3 miles two small tarns frame Mount Shuksan and mark the usual turnaround.

There is no water: the tarns are shallow and silty. Carry everything from the car.
hazards: An exposed catwalk cut into a cliff band with 400-800 ft drops and loose gravel underfoot
Snow or verglas in the cliff band into July, which is the usual reason parties turn back
Braided use-trails on a flat plateau, the classic place to lose direction in cloud
No water — the summit tarns are shallow and silty
Beyond the tarns the tread degrades into an unmaintained scramble toward the glacier

name: West Ridge Scramble
approach: From the Barclay Lake Trailhead (2,300 ft, ~20-car lot with privy), walk about a quarter mile back down the road to a short spur road and follow it down to Barclay Creek — as of spring 2026 the footlog crossing has been removed for safety with no announced replacement, so expect a rock-hop or ford. Pick up an unmaintained climbers' path up Tailgunner Creek/Tailgunner Ravine; it's brushy with blowdown lower down and passes through a short waterfall ravine before reaching the base of the Tailgunner Couloir. Follow the couloir (steep snow in spring/early summer) to Tailgunner Pass at roughly 5,320-5,400 ft. The round trip is roughly 6-7 miles with about 3,600 ft of gain for Tailgunner alone, and up to about 6,000 ft when Gunn Peak or Wing Peak are combined — budget a long day (8+ hours car-to-car) or plan an overnight camp near the pass.
descent: Reverse the west ridge back over the gendarmes to the base of the summit block, then descend the same line used on the ascent — either downclimbing (or a short rappel through the crux band in early-season snow/cornice conditions) into the Tailgunner Couloir, or dropping the east slope toward the pass/basin if conditions favor it. A cliff band immediately north of Tailgunner Pass blocks a direct drop from the pass into Gunn Basin, so go around it to the west; carry a rope for the occasional short rappel past the corniced step.
hazards: Trail-less approach with brush, blowdown, and a currently missing Barclay Creek crossing (footlog removed in spring 2026) requiring a rock-hop or ford
Steep, often corniced snow on the Tailgunner Couloir and north slope well into early summer
Loose rock and exposure on the west-ridge gendarmes
A cliff band on the north side of Tailgunner Pass blocks direct descent — a real route-finding trap
Unreliable cell coverage and a long, technical carry-out if a rescue is needed

waysIn.name: Tailgunner Ravine to Tailgunner Pass
waysIn.season: Mid-July to September
waysIn.notes: Walk about a quarter mile back down the road from the trailhead to a short spur road, follow it down to Barclay Creek and cross — do not count on a footlog, and plan on a rock-hop or a ford. An unmaintained climbers' path then follows Tailgunner Creek, brushy with blowdown low down before firming up on more open ground around 3,600 ft. It passes a short waterfall ravine and reaches the couloir, which carries steep snow in spring and early summer. Budget a long day or camp near the pass; combining Gunn Peak or Wing Peak turns this into a much bigger outing.
hazards: Barclay Creek crossing with no reliable footlog
Steep, often corniced snow in the couloir and on the north slope into early summer
Loose rock and exposure on the west-ridge gendarmes
A cliff band on the north side of the pass that blocks a direct drop into Gunn Basin
Slick rock in the waterfall ravine when wet

name: North Couloir
approach: From the White River Trailhead (see Southeast Route access), reach the upper Whitechuck/Suiattle Glacier basin via the PCT and cross to the Honeycomb Glacier, or descend the Honeycomb Glacier northward from a high camp on Kololo Peaks (8,220 ft) further west along the Glacier Peak massif. Traverse the glacier to the col just west of Tenpeak and the base of the north couloir.
descent: From the summit, reverse the short 5.4 pitch back to the top of the couloir. Ski parties descend the couloir itself (firm corn snow in the morning softening through the day); climbers on foot downclimb the ~1,200-ft, up-to-35-degree snow to the Honeycomb Glacier and retrace the approach.
hazards: Steep, sustained couloir climbing with rockfall potential from surrounding cliff bands
Crevassed glacier approach (Honeycomb/Suiattle Glaciers)
Lightning exposure on the open upper mountain
Long, remote, multi-day approach with a difficult bailout once in the couloir

waysIn.name: Over the col west of Tenpeak and down the Honeycomb Glacier to the couloir's base
waysIn.season: Roughly Apr-Jul. This is a spring line: it wants continuous firm snow, and it has been climbed and skied as early as mid-April and as late as mid-July. By mid-summer the apron melts out and the couloir bakes to bare ice and scree
waysIn.notes: There is no short way to this side of the mountain. Parties reach it either from the White River Trailhead by way of the PCT and the upper White Chuck and Suiattle basins, or by dropping onto the Honeycomb from a high camp out on the Kololo Peaks — which is why it is most often climbed as one leg of a multi-day traverse rather than as an objective on its own. Either way the ground you cover on the day is the same: reach the col that sits immediately west of Tenpeak, cross onto the Honeycomb Glacier there, and lose height across the glacier before traversing in beneath the north side. The couloir itself is roughly 1,200 ft of snow up to about 35 degrees — a boot-and-axe climb rather than a technical one — finishing on the north-west ridge, where a single short rock pitch of about 5.4 leads to the summit. That last pitch is the reason to carry a rope on a route that otherwise does not obviously need one. This is the thinnest-documented line here. What is written here comes from a small number of accounts and this route's own record; treat the couloir's condition as unknown until you can see it.
hazards: A committing position — once in the couloir the bailout is back down 1,200 ft of snow onto a glacier, hours from anywhere
Rockfall out of the cliff bands flanking the couloir, worse as the day warms
Crevasses on the Honeycomb and the upper Suiattle basins, crossed on the way in and again on the way out
A short rock pitch at the very top that a party carrying no rope cannot protect
Lightning exposure on wholly open upper-mountain terrain with no shelter for miles

name: South Couloir (Standard Route)
approach: From the Lena Lake Trailhead (Trail #810) off FS-25 at roughly 700 ft, hike the maintained Lena Lake Trail about 3 miles and ~1,100 ft of gain through second-growth and old-growth forest, crossing several creek drainages on the way, to Lena Lake (~1,800 ft) — a popular backpacking destination with a ranger station and established campsites, and the last easy, reliable water/camping before the climbers' route. Skirt the west side of the lake and pick up the unmaintained but well-trodden 'Brothers Trail' boot path, which continues up the East Fork Lena Creek drainage through the old-growth 'Valley of the Silent Men' for roughly another 2.5-3 miles to a climbers' camp (sometimes called Camp Brothers) at about 2,900 ft, marked by a fire ring — most parties treat this as their high camp for a two-day ascent. From camp, leave the tread and follow a climbers' path along the west fork of Lena Creek for about a mile; this crosses an avalanche debris field where slide alder and downed logs (some with hand-lines/notches cut in) obscure the route and creek fords may be required — go carefully, especially with a full pack. Beyond the debris field the path re-enters forest and climbs to the base of the South Couloir around 4,000-4,300 ft. Ascend the couloir (firm snow in early season, loose scree by mid/late summer) a few hundred feet, then exit onto its west side and continue up scree to about 5,000 ft, making an ascending rightward traverse below cliff bands to reach the crest of a semi-open spur. From the spur, work up and right to the base of 'the Hourglass,' a narrow rock/snow constriction that is the technical crux of the approach to the summit block (Class 3 scrambling, or a steep 35-45° snow climb in early season requiring an axe and solid self-arrest skills — watch for a moat opening at its base as the snow recedes). Above the Hourglass, continue on scree or snow toward the summit ridge and watch closely for a cairned, easy-to-miss notch on the right (climbers describe it as a 'dwarf door' — nearly invisible until you're directly in front of it); this notch is the route-finding key to the final gully leading to the true south summit, the last roughly 200 vertical feet of which is Class 4 with real exposure. Water is reliable at Lena Lake and along Lena Creek up to high camp; above camp, plan on snowmelt or carrying water, as there's nothing reliable once you're on the scree/couloir.
descent: The standard descent reverses the ascent line exactly, and for most parties it is a downclimb with no rappelling: down-climb the exposed Class 4 summit block back through the cairned notch (some parties belay or place a single short rappel of roughly 30-50 ft here off a sling around a rock horn or chockstone if the party is inexperienced, the rock is wet, or exposure has anyone spooked — there is no fixed/bolted rappel station reported, so bring a sling/cord and be prepared to build a natural anchor if you want the extra protection), then continue down through the Hourglass with careful, deliberate downclimbing on loose Class 3 rock (this is the section most prone to kicking rockfall onto anyone below, so descend one at a time with the party grouped tightly or well spread out). Below the Hourglass, downclimb or plunge-step/glissade the scree and snow of the South Couloir back to treeline (glissading is common on lingering snow but watch for a runout onto rock or the moat near the couloir's base), then pick up the climbers' path back through the avalanche debris/slide-alder crossing, through the Valley of the Silent Men, past high camp, and back down the Brothers Trail and Lena Lake Trail to the trailhead. Overall this route has no mandatory technical rappels — it is a walk-off/downclimb — but treat the summit-block notch as an optional single-rappel section if conditions or party experience warrant it. Descent hazards include loose, exposure-prone downclimbing at the notch and through the Hourglass, rockfall onto lower party members, softening/isothermal snow in the couloir on warm afternoons (raising wet-slide and post-holing risk), and simple fatigue-driven route-finding errors re-locating the 'dwarf door' notch and the correct exit from the couloir on the way down — several trip reports flag the descent as the part where parties get off-route, not the ascent.
hazards: Rockfall in the South Couloir and at the Hourglass, worsened by other parties climbing above
Exposed, loose class 3-4 scrambling at the Hourglass with real fall consequences
Avalanche terrain in the South Couloir during snow-covered months
Faint, unmaintained climbers' path through the Valley of the Silent Men, easy to lose in fog/whiteout
Deep moats and unstable snow bridges flanking the Hourglass into early summer

waysIn.name: Lena Lake and the Brothers climbers' path (summer)
waysIn.season: Jun-Sep; by late August the couloir is often scrambling rather than snow
waysIn.notes:
Lena Lake Trailhead (Trail #810) off FS-25, around 700 ft. About 3 miles and 1,100 ft of gain on maintained trail through second- and old-growth, crossing several creek drainages, to Lena Lake at roughly 1,800 ft — a busy backpacking destination with a ranger station, and the last easy reliable water and camping before the climbers' route.

Skirt the west side of the lake and pick up the unmaintained but well-trodden Brothers boot path, which follows the East Fork Lena Creek drainage through the old-growth known as the Valley of the Silent Men for roughly 2.5-3 miles to a climbers' camp around 2,900 ft, marked by a fire ring. Most parties use this as high camp for a two-day ascent.

Route-finding gets hardest immediately after leaving camp for the summit push, where the boot path repeatedly appears to vanish. Follow a climbers' path upstream and west along the west fork for about a mile. It crosses an avalanche debris field where slide alder and downed logs — some with hand-lines or steps cut into them — hide the line, and creek fords may be needed. Beyond the debris field the path re-enters forest and climbs toward the couloir.

Water is reliable at the lake and up Lena Creek to high camp. Above camp there is nothing dependable once you are on scree and snow.
hazards: avalanche debris field of slide alder and downed logs between high camp and the couloir, with possible creek fords
moat opening at the base of the Hourglass as the snow recedes
thin snow bridge through the Hourglass constriction in spring
misleading cairns on the upper route
class 4 with real exposure on the last 200 ft
no reliable water above high camp
waysIn.whyThisWay: Once the snow has gone, from about July, when the couloir is a loose scree slog and the boot path is visible, though the gullies are brushier.

waysIn.name: Early-season snow ascent
waysIn.season: Apr-May, snow
waysIn.notes:
The classic time for this route is early season, roughly April into May, because the gullies fill in with dense brush later and the snow-covered version is much faster.

The approach is the same — Lena Lake, the Brothers boot path up the East Fork, the climbers' camp near 2,900 ft — but the avalanche debris field between camp and the couloir is easier under snow, and the couloir itself becomes a snow climb requiring an axe and reliable self-arrest rather than a scree slog.

Snow also buries the boot path, so the route-finding difficulty immediately above camp is worse, not better: there is no tread to find at all.
hazards: avalanche hazard in the couloir and on the approach slopes
thin or collapsing snow bridge at the Hourglass
steep 35-45 degree snow requiring axe and solid self-arrest
no boot path visible under snow above high camp

name: The Devils Club
approach: Access starts on Ross Lake: from the Ross Dam trailhead on SR-20 (near milepost 134), hike the short Ross Dam Trail down to Ross Lake Resort, then take the resort's water taxi (or paddle a canoe) about 15 miles up-lake to the Little Beaver Creek dock. From the dock, follow the maintained (but lightly traveled) Little Beaver Trail west, paralleling Little Beaver Creek through cedar-fir forest with several brushy meadows and creek crossings, about 4.6-5 miles to Perry Creek Camp/Shelter, a three-sided log shelter that marks the effective end of maintained tread for climbers headed toward the Mox massif. From Perry Creek Camp there is no trail: the standard line follows the Perry Creek drainage south, and staying in or right beside the creekbed itself gives the fastest travel (easy rock-hopping and scrambling) up to about 3,600 ft, where dense slide alder chokes the creek and forces climbers up onto a bank. The south (true left) side of the drainage is preferred here — it holds older, more open forest and fewer avalanche paths, while the north side is a nearly impenetrable slide-alder thicket. Above the alder band the forest opens into blueberry meadows and sparser timber where travel speed improves to roughly 2-3 mph, eventually gaining the upper Perry Creek/Mox basin cirque below the connecting ridge to Southeast Mox, with talus and (season-dependent) snowfields and moats guarding the final approach to the toe of the 2,400-2,500 ft East Face. This is a genuinely serious approach, not a formality: the FA party (Layton/Wolfe, 2005) needed two full days in the rain from the lake to the base — 4.5 miles of trail, then roughly 14 hours of brush and creek travel up Perry Creek — and described it as one of the worst approaches in the Cascades. Expect cold creek fords, soaked gear, torn-up skin from devil's club and slide alder (the plant the route is named for), and real route-finding judgment calls about which side of the drainage to commit to. Water is abundant the entire way (Little Beaver Creek, Perry Creek) but should be treated.
descent: The East Face is rappelled top to bottom on its own line — there is no walk-off, and no fixed/bolted rappel stations exist anywhere on the route; every anchor is natural (slung horns, chockstones/gear anchors) built on the spot, so a party needs full natural-anchor-building skill and a rack sufficient to leave gear behind. The FA party (Layton/Wolfe) rappelled the entire 2,400-2,500 ft face using two ropes tied together to maximize each rappel's reach, angling the line closer to the northeast ridge than their ascent line, especially on the lower half, to find sounder anchor rock and avoid the loosest terrain in the direct fall line. Their first rappel hung up and forced a strenuous full return to the top to free it before they could continue; from there, roughly a dozen more rappels (about 13 total) got them to the ground, finishing around 3:30 a.m. after an 18-hour continuous push from the base. At the bottom they waded back across the creek chest-deep rather than re-entering the alder/devil's club to reach their tent. Later parties should plan on a similar count (very roughly a dozen-plus rappels with a doubled/joined-rope setup) but treat that as an estimate scaled from a single documented descent, not a fixed number — anchor placement is judgment-call and can shift the rappel line and count. Expect loose, sometimes rotten rock the entire way (a defining hazard of the route), real risk of stuck ropes given the wandering natural-anchor line, and likely a night finish if the climb runs long, so headlamps and a plan for rope work in the dark should be assumed.
hazards: Extremely loose gneiss on multiple pitches — significant rockfall risk to the second and any party below
Long runouts over stacked, unstable blocks reported by the FA team
No fixed protection anywhere on the route (no bolts) — natural gear anchors only, including for the descent
Severe remoteness compounded by the brutal Perry Creek bushwhack approach; rescue would take a very long time to organize

waysIn.name: Ross Lake to the Little Beaver landing, then the Perry Creek drainage
waysIn.season: Midsummer through early autumn; the creek travel is the governing factor rather than the climbing
waysIn.notes:
Access starts on the water. From the trailhead near milepost 134 walk down to the resort and take its water taxi, or paddle, a long way up the lake to the dock at its northern end. From the dock follow the maintained but lightly travelled valley trail west, through cedar and fir with several brushy meadows and creek crossings, to a camp with a three-sided log shelter - the effective end of maintained tread for climbers headed toward this massif.

Beyond the shelter there is no trail. This is a genuinely serious approach and not a formality: the first ascent party needed two full days in the rain from the lake to the base - four and a half miles of trail, then roughly fourteen hours of brush and creek travel - and described it as one of the worst approaches in the range. Expect cold fords, soaked gear, and skin torn by devil's club and slide alder - the plant the route is named for. Water is everywhere and should be treated.
hazards: a water taxi or a paddle up a long lake with no road out, fixing both ends of the trip
cold creek fords and continuously wet travel
devil's club and slide alder dense enough to stop progress on the wrong bank
avalanche paths on the north side of the drainage
moats between snowfield and rock at the toe of the face
a base days from any road with a very long retreat

name: Sawtooth Range Scramble
approach: Drive Hwy 101 to Hoodsport, then SR-119 (North Lake Cushman Road, becomes FR-24 past the lake) roughly 9 miles to the Staircase Ranger Station/trailhead (~800 ft) in the SE corner of Olympic National Park. Hike the North Fork Skokomish River Trail ~3.4 miles to the Spike Camp junction, then climb steeply another ~3.6 miles to Flapjack Lakes (~4,000 ft, 8 miles from the trailhead) — a limited-entry wilderness camping zone, so reserve a permit well ahead. From Flapjack Lakes, follow the Gladys Divide trail to about 4,400 ft, then leave it and climb cross-country southeast toward Sawtooth Pass to reach the base of The Fin and The Horn. Round-trip approach mileage to Gladys Divide alone runs close to 19 miles with roughly 4,000+ ft of net gain, before the additional ridge travel and the climb itself — this is realistically a backpack-in with a high camp, not a day trip from the road.
descent: Descend by rappelling from the summit notch — carrying two ropes allows a full double-rope rappel back down to the notch south of The Horn — then reverse the scramble under The Fin's west face to regain the ridge. Parties completing the fuller Sawtooth Ridge traverse have described the eventual descent off the ridge system as a brushy, slow 'controlled fall' through slide alder and devil's club; expect the broader cross-country return to Flapjack Lakes/Gladys Divide to be vegetated and time-consuming regardless of exact line.
hazards: Runout, sparsely protected 5.5 R pitches — not a route to fall on
Rock gets progressively looser/chossier toward Sawtooth Pass, especially late season
Brushy, slow approach and descent travel (slide alder, devil's club) off-trail near the ridge
Active Bear Gulch Fire burn-scar hazard (rockfall, treefall, landslides) along the Staircase/North Fork Skokomish approach corridor, the reason for the current closure
Long, remote approach — any rescue would be slow; carry a satellite communicator
Mosquitoes can be relentless in the high basins in mid-summer

waysIn.name: Sawtooth crest traverse under The Fin's west face
waysIn.season: Late July to September; ice in gullies
waysIn.notes: Same long walk in as the rest of the ridge: Staircase, the North Fork Skokomish, the steep haul to Flapjack Lakes, and on toward Gladys Divide, with a reserved overnight permit for the lakes basin arranged well in advance. Short of the divide, near a small pond at about 4,400 ft, you leave the tread for an open snow-and-rock slope climbing southeast toward Sawtooth Pass; it commonly holds snow into midsummer, so an axe earns its weight on an early trip. Below the pass, a loose, exposed class 3-4 traverse leads right under The Fin's west face. Do not read the modest grade as a scramble — the summit pitch is run-out and the rock wants careful placements. Confirm the Skokomish approach trails are open before you go; fire damage has closed them for long stretches.
hazards: Run-out, sparsely protected fifth-class climbing on the summit pitch — not a route to fall on
Rock quality falls off steadily as you move toward Sawtooth Pass, and worsens as snow melts off the ledges
The traverse under The Fin's west face is exposed and loose, with poor footing and nothing to catch a slip
Two ropes are wanted for the rappel back into the notch, and the anchors are slung rather than bolted
Slide alder and devil's club on any off-crest return line
Very long and remote — any rescue would take days, so carry a satellite communicator

name: The L & H Route (Free Variation)
approach: M&M Wall, also known as Supercave Wall for the tennis-court-sized cave crossing the cliff at mid-height, is one of the largest roadside walls at Washington Pass. Park at a pullout near milepost 166 on SR-20, about 3 miles east of the hairpin turns (and a similar distance from the Washington Pass summit). From the highway, head directly uphill toward the talus at the base of the Supercave gully, following it up and briefly left before rejoining the gully; it takes roughly 1 hour to reach the lower ledge and about 1 hour 10 minutes to reach the upper ledge and base of the longer routes.
descent: From the top, rappel down the Ellen Pea line using two ropes (diagonal rappelling is required in places), or walk down via the 3rd-class terrain to the west.
hazards: Old fixed pitons remain from the 1969 aid ascent in places; treat as unreliable.
Cave traversal on pitch 5 exposes climbers to loose rock and cold, damp rock.
Route grades are "theoretical" due to very few repeat ascents — expect route-finding uncertainty.

waysIn.name: Supercave gully to the shared start at the foot of the wall
waysIn.season: June to September, once the gully is clear; no access while the highway over the pass is gated for winter.
waysIn.notes: Same walk-in as the wall's other long routes: from the pullout near milepost 166 go straight uphill into the talus below the gully, out left where it forces you, back into the gully, past the lower ledge, and on to the upper ledge. Allow more time than the distance suggests — the ground is talus, loose, and steepens near the top.
hazards: Loose talus in the approach gully and rockfall from parties above
Old fixed pitons from the original aid ascent remain in place and must not be trusted
Very few repeat ascents, so expect route-finding uncertainty from the first pitch onward
The cave traverse higher up holds loose rock and stays cold and damp

name: Ridge Traverse Route
approach: From the Goodell Creek Trailhead off the North Cascades Highway (SR-20) near Newhalem, follow the Goodell Creek climbers' path, crossing two branches of the creek before a steep, cairned ascent (roughly 4 miles in) into the Terror Creek drainage. From there, either climb the steep Terror Basin route (about 2.5 miles, ~4,700 ft gain, faint tread, dense brush, and a class 3 root-pull section at a cliff band) or take the more direct but notoriously brushy Crescent Creek Basin line to reach a high camp below The Rake's east ridge. Expect a long, unmarked, bushwhack-heavy day-plus approach typical of the Pickets — there is no maintained trail.
descent: There is no walk-off descent. Parties rappel the east ridge back toward the Crescent Creek side, or, when climbing The Rake mid-traverse, continue over talus and snow below the Twin Spires to a camp on the west side before proceeding toward Himmelhorn.
hazards: Loose, rubble-filled gully directly below the route's initial vertical/overhanging rock — the main rockfall hazard
Sustained, exposed climbing along a narrow, serrated ridge crest with limited retreat options
Remote, glaciated approach terrain in the Terror/Crescent Creek basins — crevasse and steep snow hazard, especially early season
Fast-changing North Cascades weather; rain or snow can move in within hours even in mid-summer

waysIn.name: Crescent Creek Basin to the Terror col
waysIn.season: Mid-July to September, once the basins are melted out enough to camp and travel
waysIn.notes: From the Goodell Creek trailhead follow the climbers' path up the old roadbed, crossing two branches of the creek, then take the steep cairned ascent into the Terror Creek drainage. Either climb the Terror Basin line — faint tread, dense brush and a class 3 root-pull section at a cliff band — or the more direct but notoriously brushy Crescent Creek Basin line, to a high camp beneath the peak. There is no maintained trail anywhere on this approach and it is a long day or more of unmarked bushwhacking.
hazards: Rubble-choked entry gully with continuous rockfall potential
Very steep rock immediately off the notch, with old fixed pins rather than modern anchors
About half a mile of serrated alpine ridge above, with committing terrain and no easy escape

name: The Scoop
approach: Start at the Stuart Lake Trailhead (NF-7601 off Icicle Creek Road; NW Forest Pass required) and follow the Stuart Lake Trail (#1599) roughly 2.25 miles, crossing Mountaineer Creek on a log bridge near the 1.5-mile mark, to the junction where the Colchuck Lake Trail (#1599A) branches left. Stay on #1599A across a second Mountaineer Creek log crossing and up steepening, rocky switchbacks to Colchuck Lake (about 4 miles and 2,280 ft of gain, roughly 1:45-2:00 hiking). From the lake, reach Colchuck Balanced Rock's west basin either via the shorter northern line — cross the lake's outlet below the small dam at the north end and follow a climbers' path across timbered hillside straight into the cirque (about an hour, plus ~20-25 minutes boulder-hopping the talus to the actual base) — or the longer southern/Aasgard line, following the lakeshore path counter-clockwise toward the Aasgard Pass slopes, cutting north through a slide-alder band (cairned) into the leftmost gully, climbing that ~1,000 ft to its top, then contouring east on an easy path into the basin (1.5-2 hours, more gain but no ford). The Scoop starts in the basin to the right of the West Face and the Tempest, left of Rikki Tikki Tavi — from the base of the wall, the first three pitches (up to 5.10a) lead to 'Launch Ledge,' the platform below the namesake Scoop corner pitch. Colchuck Lake is the last dependable water source; carry what you need for a long climbing day. Hazards mirror the West Face approach: slick/high log-bridge creek crossings early season, a real bushwhack through slide alder, loose gully talus, and lingering snow into early summer on the gully and basin.
descent: Parties who top out can use CBR's standard descent shared with the West Face: a single 30 m rappel east from a slung horn, then scree or snow clockwise around the peak to the base. The alternative, which avoids that loose ground, is to rappel the route itself: with two 60m ropes tied together, descend via a sequence of natural anchors — slung trees and horns down the crack systems below Launch Ledge — there are no bolts or fixed gear anywhere on the route, by design, so you are relying entirely on what you find or build (extra slings/cord are worth carrying). Watch for rope-snag risk in the corner systems on the crux Scoop pitch and loose rock low in the gully system if you bail before topping out. No count of rappels down the route itself is published; the route is about 1,000 ft over 10 pitches, so expect a long series, and be ready to build or equalize a natural anchor if a station looks marginal.
hazards: Loose rock typical of the formation

waysIn.name: Colchuck Lake outlet into the west cirque
waysIn.season: Jul-Sep
waysIn.notes:
Stuart Lake Trailhead (NF-7601 off Icicle Creek Road; Northwest Forest Pass). Stuart Lake Trail #1599 for roughly 2.25 miles with a Mountaineer Creek log bridge near 1.5 miles, to the junction where Colchuck Lake Trail #1599A branches left; a second Mountaineer Creek log crossing, then steepening rocky switchbacks to Colchuck Lake — about 4 miles and 2,280 ft, roughly one and three-quarter to two hours for a fit party.

The shorter line into the west basin: cross the lake's outlet below the small dam at the north end and follow the climbers' path up and across the timbered hillside straight into the cirque — about an hour from the lake, plus 15 to 25 minutes of boulder-hopping to the wall. Colchuck Lake is the last dependable water; carry what you need for a long day.
hazards: Slick or partly submerged log bridges over Mountaineer Creek early season
Loose talus in the basin and the final scramble
No water above Colchuck Lake
Snow lingering in the basin into early summer

waysIn.name: Aasgard-side lakeshore, slide alder, leftmost gully
waysIn.season: Jul-Sep; ice axe useful before mid-July
waysIn.notes: Follow the lakeshore climbers' path counter-clockwise toward the Aasgard Pass slopes, gaining talus and heather about 400 ft above the lake, then cut north through the slide-alder band — cairned, but a genuine bushwhack of 15 to 20 minutes. Take the left-most gully and climb it about 1,000 ft to its top, then contour east on an easy path into the basin. One and a half to two hours from the lake, more gain than the outlet line but no ford.
hazards: Wet snow on the Aasgard slope into July
Dense slide alder
Loose gully talus; late snow in the gully
waysIn.whyThisWay: When the lake outlet is hard to cross, or to avoid a ford altogether, at the cost of a slide-alder bushwhack and a longer, steeper climb up the gully.

name: West Side
approach: From the Snow Lakes Trailhead on Icicle Creek Road (about 4.2 mi from US-2, ~1,300 ft elevation), cross Icicle Creek on the trail bridge and begin the long, switchbacking climb up open, sun-baked slabs on Snow Lakes Trail No. 1553 — this lower stretch is notoriously hot with almost no shade, so carry more water than feels necessary for the first few miles. The grade eases as the trail enters the hanging valley and reaches Nada Lake at roughly 5.5-5.6 miles (~5,000 ft), banking most of the day's approach mileage but only a bit over half the total gain. Follow the trail/use path along the lake's west shore past scattered campsites to Nada Creek near the lake's upper end — a boulder-hop in normal summer flow, but a genuine ford in early-season high water. Immediately past the creek, leave the maintained trail: climb a cairned climbers' path staying along the south edge of a broad talus field toward the notch that opens into Temple Canyon. Where the talus narrows to roughly 75 ft, work right onto a class 2-3 ledge system that skirts a waterfall, then continue up slabs into scattered trees. A steep, loose dirt-and-rock climbers' path then leads into Temple Canyon proper, staying near the stream (the last reliable water before the summit block) as it steepens toward the canyon head. Near the top, scramble up and left onto the broad, larch-dotted plateau of Tamarack Meadows (~6,600 ft), cross another talus/boulder field above treeline, and follow a final sandy ramp under an overhang to the base of the South Ridge's technical section. Figure roughly 8 miles and ~7,000 ft one-way from the trailhead to the 8,295 ft summit — about 16-16.5 miles round trip, a very long car-to-car day if not camping at Nada Lake or in the canyon. Hazards: sustained sun exposure with no shade on the lower switchbacks, an unbridged Nada Creek crossing that gets serious with early-season snowmelt, faint cairn-dependent route-finding above Nada Lake, loose talus and scree throughout Temple Canyon, and lingering snow on north-facing ledges into early summer.
descent: Because the South Ridge is cliffed-out on multiple sides, parties descend by downclimbing and rappelling the same south-side line used on the ascent rather than walking off. From the summit block, the first rappel drops off a fixed station just below the top — parties describe a single old, not-fully-confidence-inspiring bolt/pin anchor here, so back it up with a cam or nut if you have any doubt — down past the 5.3-5.6 friction slab crux to a ledge. From there, most parties make one further rappel through a band of loose rock and boulders to a notch where the anchor is natural: a sling around a large wedged chockstone (some parties have refreshed this with a new sling and rap ring). A single 60m rope rappelled doubled (~30m per pitch) is generally sufficient, but at least one party found the rope only just reached the next station, so treat 60m as a minimum, knot your rope ends, and expect some parties to break the descent into three shorter rappels instead of two depending on the exact gully line and rope length carried. After the last rappel, downclimb and plunge-step the loose gully below the rockfall zone back onto the ascent talus, then retrace the approach through Temple Canyon, Tamarack Meadows, and the climbers' path back to Nada Lake and the Snow Lakes Trail. Wear a helmet throughout the descent — the gully channels loose rock kicked down by parties above. In May-June the steep upper snow gully below the notch was rappelled from existing stations, then downclimbed or plunge-stepped; extra rap anchors already line the approach slabs.
hazards: Loose, blocky rock on the approach ledges and near the summit block
Exposed class 4 scrambling plus a low-5th-class (5.3-5.6) crux slab move protected by only a single, aging bolt
Long, complex off-trail approach through Temple Canyon requiring real route-finding
Lingering snow and steep gullies into early summer, requiring an ice axe and crampons in June/early July
Afternoon thunderstorms in July-August
Very long round trip (~16 miles, 7,000-8,000 ft gain) that leads to fatigue-related mistakes on the descent

waysIn.name: Snow Lakes trail, Nada Lake and Temple Canyon
waysIn.season: July to September; axe in June
waysIn.notes: A very long day from the road even for fit parties. The lower Snow Lakes trail switchbacks up open, sun-baked slabs with almost no shade, so carry more water than feels sensible; the grade eases into the hanging valley at Nada Lake around five and a half miles. Follow the west shore to the creek at the lake's upper end, a boulder-hop in normal flow and a genuine ford in early-season melt, and leave the maintained trail immediately past it. A cairned climbers' path runs along the south edge of a broad talus field toward the notch into Temple Canyon; where the talus narrows to roughly seventy-five feet, work right onto a ledge system that skirts a waterfall, then up slabs into scattered trees. A steep, loose path leads into the canyon proper — stay near the stream, which is the last reliable water below the summit block.
hazards: Loose, blocky rock on the approach ledges and along the ridge, with large poised blocks near the summit block
A rockfall zone directly below the start of the technical ground — do not linger under it
Exposed class 4 scrambling and a short low-fifth-class crux protected by a single aged bolt
Faint, cairn-dependent route-finding above Nada Lake
Lingering snow on north-facing ledges and in the gullies into early summer
Old rappel anchors and slings that periodically need replacing — carry spare webbing

name: The Tipping Point
approach: Standard Colchuck Balanced Rock approach via Colchuck Lake and the Aasgard Pass gully; the route is to the left of Let It Burn and the West Face.
descent: After topping out via Let it Burn’s upper pitches, take the standard summit descent: an optional single rappel of about 30 m from a slung horn, then scree or snow clockwise around the peak back to the base. To retreat from the lower half instead, rappel to the Sky Lounge, the two-bolt ledge atop pitch 3, stopping first at the Kerwin’s Crack anchor if your rope does not reach it in one; from the Sky Lounge, two rappels of about 40 m each return to the approach gully. Those need two ropes or an 80 m rope; a single 60 m rope folded double reaches only 30 m.
hazards: Loose rock typical of the formation

waysIn.name: Colchuck Lake, the Aasgard trail, then left through the brush to the base gully
waysIn.season: Roughly Jul-Sep; the traverse above the lake holds wet snow into July and has produced serious slips
waysIn.notes: From the Stuart Lake trailhead on FR 7601, take the Stuart Lake Trail #1599 toward Colchuck Lake — four miles and 2,280 ft, a log-bridge crossing of Mountaineer Creek at about 1.5 miles, left at the Lake Stuart junction onto the Colchuck Lake Trail #1599A, then a boulder-moraine finish to the outlet in about two and a half to three hours. Fill water here; it is the last source. Head round toward the lake's south and east side onto the cairned Aasgard Pass climbers' trail and gain talus and heather to about 400 ft above the lake, thirty to forty minutes. Then leave it: break climber's left through a dense band of slide alder and heather, fifteen to twenty minutes of real bushwhacking, to the obvious gully leading up to Colchuck Balanced Rock. The final scramble to the wall is loose third and fourth class; rope up if in doubt. Reckon three and a half to four hours car to base.
hazards: A wet-snow traverse above Colchuck Lake into July with a history of serious slips
Fifteen to twenty minutes of dense slide alder and heather to reach the gully
Loose third and fourth class scrambling in the base gully with parties above
No water above Colchuck Lake
Above the fourth-pitch anchor there is no rappel retreat — the route must be finished
A long walk-off round the peak after topping out

name: The Tooth Fairy
approach: Same Alpental to Snow Lake Trail to Source Lake fork to Pineapple Pass approach as the standard Tooth routes (~3,100 ft trailhead); near the top, continue left past the Southwest Face to a bolted line on the west-facing wall. Early season, a moat between snow and rock may require extra scrambling to the start.
descent: From the top of P6 (the anchor is unequipped at the true summit — P7 is a short scramble with no rappel anchor), rappel the bolted line: 6 single-rope rappels, or 3 double-rope rappels with a 60m rope for the longest one. Some parties instead go down the South Face, rappelling its line to Pineapple Pass.
hazards: Rockfall exposure where routes converge near the summit
Snow moat at the base in early season
Scrambling with a single bolt above the last bolted anchor to reach the true summit

waysIn.name: Standard Tooth approach, then left past the Southwest Face
waysIn.season: Jul-Sep
waysIn.notes: Identical to the South Face approach as far as Great Scott Bowl: Alpental upper lot, Snow Lake Trail about 1.5-1.6 miles to the Source Lake junction, bear left, cross the Source Lake basin near 4,000 ft, crest the lip into Great Scott Bowl around 4,400 ft, and climb the bowl toward Pineapple Pass beneath the Fang. Rather than finishing at the notch south of the pass and contouring to the South Face, this line stays lower and further left (west), working past the Southwest Face along the base of the west-facing wall. The Fang is the formation that catches people out. A boot path around its back side leads up into the gully between the Fang and the Tooth; from there, getting to the Tooth Fairy means backtracking down and picking a way through rough climbers' paths in the trees and across the rock fields.
hazards: moat between snow and rock at the base in early season
loose talus in Great Scott Bowl
rockfall from parties on the South Face and Southwest Face above and right
the boot path behind the Fang leads to the wrong gully

name: South Face (Standard)
approach: From the Alpental (Snow Lake) trailhead at the end of Alpental Road (~3,100–3,250 ft), follow the Snow Lake Trail (Trail #1013) north for about 2 miles, climbing steadily through forest to roughly 4,100 ft, where a small signed junction splits the Source Lake fork from the Snow Lake fork (bear toward Source Lake). Watch on your left as the trail curves for the point where a continuous talus field begins running alongside it — this is where you leave the maintained tread. Cut off-trail into the talus and traverse west, dropping slightly at first, then climbing back up toward The Tooth's obvious south-facing wall, working up through Great Scott Bowl (Pineapple Basin) by whatever line of least resistance through talus and/or lingering snow. Aim for the gully just left (south) of a prominent pointed rock formation partway up the basin; in early season this slope is a steep, sustained snow climb that can warrant an axe and even crampons. The bowl funnels up to the notch/saddle between The Tooth and a smaller pinnacle immediately south of it — Pineapple Pass (~5,400 ft) — reached after crossing a moat at the top of the snow that can be tricky and, depending on the year, corniced; probe it carefully or look for a rock detour around its edge. From the pass, a short, unexposed Class 3–4 scramble contours clockwise around the south side of The Tooth to the start of the South Face route. Figure 2–3 hours and roughly 2,300–2,500 ft of gain car-to-base (one trip report logged 4.0 mi / 2,450 ft for the full day including the descent). There's no reliable water past the trailhead area/Source Lake outlet, so carry what you need — the loose talus underfoot and the upper snow-slope/moat crossing are the two spots that most commonly slow down or catch out unprepared parties.
descent: Most parties reverse the South Face itself: four rappels straight back down the face to Pineapple Pass on a single 60m rope (used doubled — each rappel comes in under 30m). The stations are natural anchors kept well equipped with fixed slings, cord and rap rings: from the top down, a station with three rap rings backed by slings/cord around a tree or horn, then an 8mm doubled cordelette with two quicklinks, then two slung trees, then a lowest station with several slings and three rap rings around a block. A second, less-crowded rappel line exists on the southwest side with bolted chain-and-ring anchors, built specifically so ascending and descending parties don't have to share the same gully — also doable on a single 60m rope in a similar number of rappels. Once back at Pineapple Pass, the safest and most common way out is to skip further rappelling and simply reverse the Class 3–4 scramble and talus/snow descent through Great Scott Bowl back to the Source Lake junction on the Snow Lake Trail, then walk the 2 miles out to Alpental — this avoids rockfall exposure and is usually faster for parties larger than two. A separate bail option drops climbers from Pineapple Pass down the East Gully via two rappels off bolted chain anchors (single 60m rope) directly toward the Source Lake basin, but that gully sees rockfall from above and from parties climbing up it, so it's generally treated as an emergency/bail line rather than the standard way down. The moat/snow bridge at the base of the pass can again be the crux of the whole descent in early season — downclimb carefully or detour onto rock.
hazards: Heavy weekend crowding — widely cited as WA's most popular alpine rock climb, causing queues on the route and at rappels
Snow moat at the Pineapple Pass notch up to ~8 ft deep in early season
Rockfall in the rappel/descent gully, worsened by parties climbing above
Aging tree anchors at some belay/rappel stations
Afternoon thunderstorms possible in July-August

waysIn.name: Snow Lake Trail to Great Scott Bowl and Pineapple Pass
waysIn.season: Jul-Sep (snow-free)
waysIn.notes: Upper Alpental lot at the end of Alpental Road (about 3,100 ft), I-90 exit 52. Take the Snow Lake Trail (#1013) north; a cat track runs up the valley from the end of the lot, just left of the stream, before the tread narrows to normal trail. At roughly 1.5-1.6 miles a small signed junction splits Source Lake from Snow Lake — bear left toward Source Lake. Cross the Source Lake basin contouring near 4,000 ft, then at about 4,400 ft you crest a lip and drop into Great Scott Bowl (also called Pineapple Basin). Work up the bowl on talus, or on snow if any remains, toward Pineapple Pass at the head of it, passing beneath the Fang — the pinnacle on the bowl's west side that carries the Edge of Time route. The common error is here, not lower down: a boot path running around the back of the Fang leads into the gully between the Fang and the Tooth. Parties who take it have to backtrack several hundred feet through trees and rock fields to get back onto the right ground. The second error is going straight up to Pineapple Pass itself — that col is the rappel line down, not the way up.
hazards: loose talus underfoot the whole length of Great Scott Bowl
steep sustained snow slope below Pineapple Pass in early season - axe, sometimes crampons
moat, and in some years a cornice, where the bowl's snow meets rock at the pass
rockfall from parties above on a face that is often busy
no reliable water past the Source Lake outlet

waysIn.name: Winter and spring, snow-covered Alpental valley
waysIn.season: winter to early summer, snow
waysIn.notes: Once there is meaningful snow the summer tread is not the route. The talus slopes the summer trail crosses are the Alpental valley's avalanche chutes — seventeen of them are counted along its length — and the winter line instead climbs the valley on the south side of the South Fork Snoqualmie toward Source Lake rather than following the summer switchbacks across those paths. From below Source Lake, traverse up into Great Scott Bowl, typically on an upward-traversing line on the west side of the bowl passing beneath the Fang, and join whatever track leads to Pineapple Pass. Most parties cache skis or snowshoes in the bowl before the final slope. The entire trip through the Source Lake and Snow Lake basins is avalanche terrain; this is a stability decision, not a route-finding one.
hazards: avalanche terrain the full length of the Alpental valley - roughly seventeen chutes cross the summer trail line
the summer boot path is not a safe winter line once snow is present
cornices at Pineapple Pass
moat between the snow and the rock at the top of the bowl
creek crossings near the Source Lake outlet at high early-season flow
waysIn.whyThisWay: Once snow buries the summer trail, when the usual talus slopes become avalanche paths and the party travels the valley floor toward Source Lake instead.

name: East Peak (Standard Route)
approach: From Marblemount, drive Cascade River Road (FR-15) about 10.2 paved miles, then turn onto FR-1540 (Sibley Creek Road) and follow its rough gravel surface 4.5 miles to the small Hidden Lake Trailhead (~3,600 ft; Northwest Forest Pass required to park). Hike Hidden Lake Trail #745 through forest and wildflower meadows to about 5,400 ft, where the maintained trail begins a long traverse; leave the trail here and climb steep meadow and heather slopes to 6,200-ft Sibley Creek Pass. From the pass, a boot path follows the crest of a grassy ridge before dropping onto the Triad Glacier, which is crossed -- often on rock-hard ice under a thin snow layer -- past all three Triad summits to East Triad Col. This is a full, long approach day (roughly 6+ miles with significant elevation gain and loss) and is typically done as part of a multi-day trip with a high camp near Sibley Creek Pass or on the glacier apron.
descent: Reverse the route: downclimb and make two 30 m rappels (rope plus tagline) off the East Peak's east ridge back to East Triad Col, then re-cross the Triad Glacier roped up (watch for open crevasses, especially in late season) back to Sibley Creek Pass, and descend the boot path/meadows to Hidden Lake Trail #745 and the trailhead.
hazards: Crevasses on the Triad and Eldorado Glaciers, especially with thin or icy early/late-season cover
Loose rock and rockfall potential on the class 4-5.4 step near East Triad Col, particularly with other parties above
Complex terrain among the three closely spaced Triad summits that is easy to misjudge in fog or whiteout
Steep, brushy off-trail terrain between about 5,400 ft and Sibley Creek Pass
Heavy, wet Cascade snowpack creates high avalanche danger on the Sibley Creek approach slopes outside summer

waysIn.name: Sibley Creek Pass and the north-side glacier
waysIn.season: Roughly July to September, gated by the gravel road in and by snow on the ridge and glacier edge
waysIn.notes: From the Hidden Lake Trailhead hike the maintained trail through forest and wildflower meadows to about 5,400 ft, where it begins a long traverse; leave it there and climb steep meadow and heather to Sibley Creek Pass. From the pass a boot path follows a grassy ridge crest before dropping onto the small glacier on the peaks' north side, which is crossed past all three summits — often on rock-hard ice under a thin skin of snow — to the col at the east end. This is a full approach day and is normally done with a high camp near the pass or on the glacier apron.
hazards: Hard ice under thin snow on the glacier crossing — crampons
A steep, loose gully of dirt and rock lying on top of steeper rock and heather drops to the base
Sparse protection on the short exposed pinnacle pitch to the true summit

name: North Peak
approach: FR 41 is closed to vehicles at the Canyon Creek bridge, so first walk or bike roughly 8-9 miles of road to the trailhead. The climb starts at the Tupso Pass trailhead on the Three Fingers-Goat Flats-Saddle Lake Trail #641. The trail climbs through forest, crossing a couple of small seasonal streams, to Saddle Lake at about 2.5 miles (last reliable, easy water before the alpine section; no camping within 200 ft of the lake and no fires from here on). From Saddle Lake continue roughly 2–2.5 more miles, gaining out of the timber into the open meadows of Goat Flats (~4.5 mi from the TH) — good camps and the last easy tentsites with views to Puget Sound. From Goat Flats the trail contours and climbs about 2 more miles to Tin Can Gap (~6.2 mi, roughly 3,500-3,800 ft of the day's gain done); this is the last maintained-trail point and the standard high camp/bivy for peak days. Tin Can Gap gives the first real view of the three summits and the Queest-Alb (Three Fingers) Glacier below. From the gap the route drops about 400 ft off-trail down snow/talus onto the glacier — early season this is a straightforward snow descent, but by late summer expect bare ice and a moat between rock and ice that requires care (crampons/axe recommended into at least July); crevasses open on the glacier by mid-summer so rope up if traveling as a team when covered. Cross the glacier and climb back up roughly 1,000 ft on the far side to the col between Middle and North Peak — this climb is on a mix of snow/scree and low-angle rock and is the route-finding crux of the approach. From the col, the North Peak route follows a ramp leading left then angling right into a shallow chimney, with sustained 4th-class and a few low-5th-class (5.0-5.4) exposed moves through loose-to-fair rock to the summit block; a harder 5.4 line exists on the upper west face but is avoided by most parties for rock quality. Carry a rope, a small rack, and glacier gear (axe/crampons, and a rope+harness for crevasse hazard) even in a scramble-grade season. Water at Saddle Lake is poor; a better stream runs about halfway from there to Goat Flats, and melt streams are good beyond Tin Can Gap in late summer.
descent: Reverse the ascent line off the North Peak summit. Parties describe two to three rappels getting back down through the 4th/low-5th-class chimney-and-ramp section to easier 3rd-class ground above the glacier — plan on a single 60m rope (or two ropes if parties want to link stations in fewer pulls). The first rappel station is commonly an old fixed sling/tat anchor left by previous parties, but it should not be trusted blindly — inspect it or back it up, and be prepared to build natural gear anchors (cams/nuts on horns or cracks) for the remaining stations since fixed gear is inconsistent year to year. After the rappels, downclimb/scramble the remaining 3rd-class terrain back to the col, reverse the ~1,000 ft descent to the glacier, re-cross the Queest-Alb Glacier (watch the moat and any crevasses), climb back up to Tin Can Gap, and reverse Trail #641 through Goat Flats and Saddle Lake to the trailhead. Rockfall in the chimney/gully and a icy glacier moat are the main descent-specific hazards; a mid-to-late-season descent in soft/rotten snow on the glacier headwall can also be tricky.
hazards: Glacier travel with real crevasse risk crossing to the North/Middle col
Loose rock in the chimney/ramp system
No established trail or cairned route — routefinding is on you
Committing rappel descent with only fixed-anchor slings of unknown age at some stations

waysIn.name: Trail #641 from Tupso Pass over Goat Flats and Tin Can Gap
waysIn.season: July to September. Crevasses open on the glacier by midsummer and bare ice with a moat appears late in the season; an axe is a year-round item on this peak.
waysIn.notes: Note the access before anything else: the road up to the historic trailhead has a permanent washout, so the day starts with a long bike or walk past the vehicle gate before the trail proper begins. From the trailhead, the trail climbs through forest to the small lake at about two and a half miles — last easy water, and no fires or camping within two hundred feet of it. Continue up into the open meadows of the flats at about four and a half miles, the best camping on the route, then a further couple of miles to the GAP at roughly six miles, where the maintained tread ends and most parties bivy. The gap gives the first real view of the three summits and of the glacier below them.
hazards: Glacier travel with real crevasse risk crossing to the col
A moat between rock and ice that widens through the season, with bare ice by late summer
Loose rock in the chimney and ramp system
No established trail or cairned route above the gap — route-finding is entirely on you
The descent is a committing series of rappels, and some stations are fixed slings of unknown age
Fog on the glacier traverse has triggered multiple multi-hour rescues on this mountain

name: South Peak via Lookout
approach: FR 41 is closed to vehicles at the Canyon Creek bridge, so first walk or bike roughly 8-9 miles of road to the trailhead. From the Tupso Pass trailhead, follow Three Fingers Trail #641 through forest to Saddle Lake (~2.5 mi, last easy water — no fires or camping within 200 ft of the lake past this point), then continue up through meadows to Goat Flats (~4.5 mi total), a broad subalpine bench with the best camping on the route and views out to Puget Sound. From Goat Flats the trail climbs roughly 2 more miles to Tin Can Gap (~6.2-7 mi total, most of the day's 4,200 ft gain banked); this is where the maintained trail effectively ends and most casual hikers turn around. Beyond the gap, drop off-trail onto the Queest-Alb (Three Fingers) Glacier — a short but real glacier crossing with a moat between ice and rock that widens through the season (crampons/axe strongly recommended, especially before August); a rope is worth carrying if crevasses are open. On the far side, scramble up rock and snow past the base of the summit block to the historic lookout's ladder system: three fixed wooden ladders bolted/pinned into the rock, stacked in sequence, gaining the final class-5-equivalent rock band to the lookout deck. The transition between the second and third ladder is the trickiest move and is awkward with a full pack; exposure is significant and a slip here would be serious, so this last pitch is why the route is rated a scramble rather than a hike despite no rope typically being used. Some parties fix or find a hand-line/rope on a short exposed rock step just past Tin Can Gap before the glacier — treat it as unverified fixed gear.
descent: This is a walk-off/downclimb route with no roped rappelling on the standard line. Downclimb the three fixed ladders in reverse (facing in, one at a time, mind the awkward 2nd-to-3rd ladder transition), then reverse the rock/snow scramble back down to and across the Queest-Alb Glacier, watching the moat and any open crevasses. Climb back up to Tin Can Gap and reverse Trail #641 through Goat Flats and Saddle Lake to the trailhead. The main descent hazards are the exposed ladder pitch (a fall here would be very serious despite no technical rappelling), a soft or icy glacier moat later in the day, and lingering steep snow on the south ridge in early season — an ice axe is recommended into mid-summer. No rappel gear is needed for the standard route.
hazards: Queest-Alb Glacier crevasses and slick ice, especially before September
Loose rock on the final scramble above the glacier
Exposed, cabled ladders with a tight, awkward transition between the 2nd and 3rd ladder
Fog/whiteout near Tin Can Gap and on the glacier traverse has triggered multiple multi-hour Snohomish County SAR rescues

The summit block is reached via three fixed wooden ladders (bolted/cabled) -- a permanent, highly exposed fixed feature; the approach crosses the Queest-Alb Glacier and steep snowfields where a slip risks a long slide into rocks, so an ice axe is required year-round

waysIn.name: Tupso Pass trailhead, Trail #641 (road drivable)
waysIn.season: Jul-Oct
waysIn.notes:
Trail #641 from the Tupso Pass trailhead at the end of FR 41. Forest to Saddle Lake at about two and a half miles — the last easy water, with no fires and no camping within two hundred feet of the shore beyond this point — then up through meadows to Goat Flats at roughly four and a half miles, which has the best camping on the route and views out to Puget Sound.

From Goat Flats the trail climbs about two more miles to Tin Can Gap at roughly six miles, banking most of the day's gain. That is the effective end of the maintained trail and where most walkers turn back.

The trail has been maintained by volunteers in recent years, with large numbers of logs cleared; note that a big fallen log above Saddle Lake has rerouted the tread, and there is a rough connector going straight up and down to the next switchback.
hazards: moat between glacier and rock that widens through the season and is hard to enter in poor visibility
crevasses on the Queest-Alb once it opens up
exposure on the ladders, particularly between the second and third
unverified fixed hand-line on the rock step past Tin Can Gap
waysIn.whyThisWay: Only if the road is ever repaired and open to vehicles again, when driving to the trailhead turns the trip from an overnight walk or bike ride into a shorter outing.

waysIn.name: Road-closure variation — walk or bike FR 41
waysIn.season: Jul-Sep
waysIn.notes:
FR 41 is closed to vehicles at the washed-out Canyon Creek bridge, leaving roughly nine miles of road between the closure and the trailhead. Vehicles are barred past the barrier but foot and bike traffic are allowed, and biking the road is the common tactic.

Treat this as a standing possibility rather than a one-off: check with the Darrington Ranger District or the Verlot Public Service Center before committing, because the difference is a day hike versus an overnight. There is now a sign at the road marking the old trailhead.
hazards: several miles of road walking or biking each way with the resulting late finish
all the hazards of the standard variation once on trail

name: Standard Scramble
