approach: Trailhead: Mineral Creek Trailhead (Trail #1331), roughly 2,360-2,400 ft, reached via FR-4600 over Cooper Pass. From the parking area the trail promptly crosses the Kachess River — look for logs spanning it; when they're not in place it's a short, easy wade. The trail then climbs gently north through second-growth and brushy old avalanche paths, muddy in spots with the occasional blowdown to step over. At about 1.6-1.7 miles it crosses Mineral Creek itself; this crossing carries enough current in early season that parties often lay a short log/rock crossing rather than ford, and the ruins of an old mine and mill sit just off-trail here as a landmark (and a fine last water source). Continue upstream through brushy trail for roughly another mile, to about the 2.7-mile mark, watching on the right (west) for a break in the timber around 3,300-3,500 ft — this is where an obvious boot/social path leaves the maintained trail and cuts west through 100-200 ft of vine-maple brush to reach the base of Three Queens' south-face talus. Leave the trail west of the broad waterfall gully that drains the south face (not the drainage directly above the creek crossing) — trip reports flag this junction as easy to get wrong in the brush. From here it's off-trail talus and scree for the remaining 1,400-1,700 ft of gain: the lower ~1,000 ft is moderately angled, largely stable large talus; above that the rock turns smaller and looser, funneling into choss gullies that run generally class 2 with short class 3 sections higher up. A snow ramp (commonly encountered around 5,200 ft) can persist into midsummer on some lines, so carry an ice axe for early-season attempts. Loose rock and rockfall are the dominant hazards through the upper talus and gullies — wear a helmet and keep the group tight so climbers aren't stacked below one another. The final ~400 ft to the 6,693-ft high point is the most exposed scrambling on the route, with brief but genuine class 3 moves and blocks that can shift underfoot; published descriptions of this section as 'class 3' are considered generous by several parties who found it heads-up the whole way.
descent: The standard descent reverses the ascent line: back down the summit scrambling, through the upper choss gullies, down the talus to the vine-maple break, and out the 2.7-2.8 miles of trail to the Mineral Creek Trailhead. No rappelling is required on this walk-off/downclimb line (rappels: 0), but the loose upper talus and gullies are generally regarded as more hazardous descending than climbing — face in through the class 3 sections, move deliberately on the small unstable talus, and regroup below rockfall lines rather than descending stacked up. Any snow ramp encountered on the ascent is often the fastest way down (plunge-step or glissade with an axe). Total time from summit to car is commonly reported around 3.5-4 hours. Note: if a party instead climbs the optional South Chimney variant (class 4, on the south face) rather than the standard talus/gully line, that route does NOT walk off — the chimney itself is descended by rappel: two rappels of about 60 ft each, reported consistently in trip logs. Anchors are natural (chockstones, horns, or slung blocks), as this is unbolted alpine rock, so carry cord/webbing to build or back up anchors. A single 60m rope handles both rappels doubled; two shorter ropes joined also work. Below the chimney, the descent rejoins the same long talus and scree slopes and the trail out. Hazards specific to this variant are loose rock in the chimney and rope-snag risk against the blocky walls.
hazards: Loose, rotten rock on both the northeast-ridge and South Chimney lines — described in trip reports as generously rated 'Class 3'
Class 5 knife-edge ridge directly connecting the Middle and East (true) summits — most parties must detour via a ledge traverse to avoid it
Persistent snow ramp on the southeast approach (roughly 4,750-5,200 ft) that can linger into July and requires care or an ice axe
River crossings (Kachess River at the trailhead, Mineral Creek below the peak) that are harder and more dangerous during high spring/early-summer flow

waysIn.name: Mineral Creek Trail to the break in the timber west of the waterfall gully
waysIn.season: July to September
waysIn.notes:
From the Mineral Creek trailhead, Trail #1331, at roughly 2,360 to 2,400 ft via FR-4600 over Cooper Pass, the trail promptly crosses the Kachess River — look for logs, and wade if they are not there. It climbs gently north through second growth and brushy old avalanche paths, muddy in places with occasional blowdown.

At about 1.6 to 1.7 miles it crosses Mineral Creek itself, which carries enough current in early season that parties often lay a log rather than ford. The ruins of an old mine and mill sit just off-trail here — a landmark and the last good water.

Continue upstream through brushy trail roughly another mile, to about the 2.7-mile mark.

About 8.85 km, with 1,400 to 1,700 ft of off-trail gain above the trail.
hazards: An unbridged Kachess River crossing at the trailhead and a Mineral Creek crossing with real current in early season
A brushy, easy-to-miss trail departure between two similar drainages
Loose rock and rockfall through the upper talus and choss gullies — helmets, and keep the group tight
A snow ramp around 5,200 ft persisting into midsummer
Brief but genuine class 3 with shifting blocks on the final 400 ft, harder than the published grade suggests

name: Southeast Ridge
approach: From the Yellow Aster Butte/Tomyhoi Lake trailhead (~3,600-3,700 ft) on Twin Lakes Road (FR 3065), start on the well-maintained Yellow Aster Butte Trail (Trail #686). The trail climbs through forest switchbacks and crosses a couple of small seasonal creeks/seep crossings in the first mile — reliable water here early season, less so by late summer. At roughly 1.5 miles you reach the signed junction with the Tomyhoi Lake Trail, which splits off to the right toward Gold Run Pass (~5,400 ft); stay left on the Yellow Aster Butte Trail. Beyond the junction the trail contours into the Yellow Aster Meadows and a basin of small tarns/lakes at about 5,200-5,600 ft (roughly 2 hours/4 miles from the car at a moderate pace) — this is the last dependable water on route. From the basin, leave the maintained trail and head north/NNW over a broad hump and down to a col around 6,266 ft, then pick up a well-defined, boot-packed climbers' path along the crest of the Tomyhoi Arm ridge. As the ridge narrows above roughly 6,800-7,000 ft, bypass the narrowest sections on broad benches on the north (right) side rather than staying on the crest. The path eventually fades into scree and talus as you approach the toe of the Tomyhoi Glacier; traverse along the top edge of the glacier (minor crevasse hazard depending on year/season — assess before committing) to avoid several rock pinnacles, aiming for a notch/moat below the false summit at about 7,250 ft. This upper section is loose, exposed, and route-finding is not obvious — expect some scrambling and sidehilling on scree and rock benches. Total approach is roughly 6-7 miles and ~3,600-3,800 ft of gain one-way from the trailhead to the base of the summit block, consistent with the ~13-14 mile, ~4,800-5,600 ft round-trip character of this route.
descent: Descend by reversing the Southeast Ridge line of ascent — there is no separate walk-off. From the true summit (7,439 ft), reverse the Class 3 summit block and the exposed ~40-ft gabled section of ridge back to the false summit, then downclimb the short wall to the notch at about 7,250 ft. This downclimb is the most exposed step on the route (big air on both sides), and many parties protect it rather than downclimbing free: previous climbing parties have left an informal rappel/lowering setup at the notch — a sling around a natural rock horn, not a bolted or fixed-chain anchor — good for one short (~15-20 ft) rappel or a doubled-rope lower/handline through the Class 3.5 slot. Inspect and back up any in-place tat before trusting it, or build your own natural anchor; a single 30m or longer rope doubled is plenty. Many parties skip the rappel entirely and instead downclimb this slot with a simple rope belay from above. Below the notch, reverse the traverse across the small snow/ice moat (can be firm or icy in morning conditions — an ice axe is worth carrying), continue back along the glacier's top edge and the north-side benches around the pinnacles, drop to the 6,266-ft col, climb back over the hump, and descend into the Yellow Aster Basin to rejoin the maintained trail. From there it's a straightforward but long descent back down the Yellow Aster Butte Trail to the trailhead; parties moving at a moderate pace should expect the descent to take nearly as long as the ascent (trip reports cite ~5 hours down), and finishing the lower trail by headlamp is common if the party is not fast.
hazards: Exposed Class 3–4 scrambling on glacier-polished rock, especially near the summit block
Loose rock in the gendarme-bypass gully — rockfall risk to parties below
Icy/hard-snow moat crossing below the summit notch requires an ice axe (crampons useful) well into summer
Route-finding: an impassable gap between the first and second gendarme forces a detour off the ridge crest; GPS tracks that show staying on the crest here are wrong and can cliff parties out

waysIn.name: Yellow Aster Butte Trail, then the Tomyhoi Arm ridge to the moat below the false summit
waysIn.season: Roughly Jun-Sep. The moat below the false summit opens as the season goes on and is the crux either way
waysIn.notes:
From the Yellow Aster Butte / Tomyhoi Lake trailhead, around 3,600-3,700 ft, on Twin Lakes Road (FR-3065), start on Yellow Aster Butte Trail #686. It climbs through forest switchbacks with a couple of seasonal creek crossings in the first mile.

At roughly 1.5 miles the signed Tomyhoi Lake Trail splits off right toward Gold Run Pass near 5,400 ft. Stay left, then contour into the Yellow Aster Meadows and a basin of small tarns at about 5,200-5,600 ft — roughly two hours and four miles from the car, and the last dependable water.

From the basin leave maintained trail: head north-northwest over a broad hump and down to a col around 6,266 ft, then pick up a well-defined boot-packed climbers' path along the crest of the Tomyhoi Arm.

As the ridge narrows above roughly 6,800-7,000 ft, bypass the narrowest sections on broad benches on the north — right — side rather than staying on the crest. The path fades into scree and talus near the toe of the Tomyhoi Glacier.
hazards: A rock-and-ice moat at the notch that is the crux of the outing and widens through the season
Glacier-polished slick rock at the snow margin
Minor crevasse hazard traversing the top edge of the Tomyhoi Glacier
Loose, exposed, non-obvious route-finding on scree and rock benches approaching the notch
The descent through the V-slot is the most exposed step of the day and is where parties rope up

name: Southwest Route / Standard
approach: Start at the Rainy Pass PCT trailhead (~4,875 ft) on SR-20, 4.7 miles west of Washington Pass. Follow the Pacific Crest Trail northbound as it switchbacks up through forest and into larch parkland to Cutthroat Pass (~6,800 ft, ~4.9 mi) — this stretch has only intermittent small streams, so fill up at the last stream below the pass, since the pass itself is dry and little reliable water exists again until Snowy Lakes. From Cutthroat Pass the PCT contours below Cutthroat Peak's west flank to Granite Pass (~6,300 ft, roughly 6.5-7 mi from the trailhead); this pass holds snow into July/August, and when snow-covered it's steep and exposed enough that an ice axe (and comfort self-arresting) is warranted. Beyond Granite Pass the trail sidehills below Tower Mountain's west side, crosses a cliff-cut, blasted-out section, and loses a bit of elevation into a meadowed basin. Roughly 9.5-10 miles in, about a mile short of Methow Pass at about 6,300 ft, a climbers'/use path branches right (east) off the PCT and climbs ~0.5 mi and ~400 ft to the Snowy Lakes basin — Lower Snowy Lake (~6,600 ft) or Upper Snowy Lake (~6,700 ft) — the standard base camp, with reliable water and good tent sites; most parties backpack in and climb from camp rather than going car-to-car. From camp near Lower Snowy Lake, head cross-country south toward Tower Mountain on a climbers' path, then make a short but strenuous traverse across a talus field, aiming for a distinctive large reddish boulder partway across. Beyond the boulder, a ramp on the left side of a large cave (which cuts about 25 yards into the mountainside and makes a good wind-sheltered rest stop) leads up to the base of the main summit gully — from here the route follows ledges on the gully's right side, zigzagging back toward the gully-notch in the ridge and up broken rock to the summit. Total distance to the base of the gully runs roughly 10-11 miles one-way with about 1,800 ft of net elevation gain from the trailhead to camp (more once the ups and downs over Cutthroat and Granite passes are counted). The gully itself is the route's main hazard: the rock is notoriously loose and rockfall-prone, so helmets are strongly recommended and parties should climb one at a time, staying right and moving efficiently through the narrowest sections. A car-to-car day from Rainy Pass is roughly 22 miles with about 5,300 ft of cumulative gain, most of it on the PCT.
descent: Descend by reversing the ascent line — this is a walk-off/downclimb with no rappelling required (rappels: 0). From the summit, downclimb back through the broken rock to the ridge notch, then follow the ramp/ledge system down the climber's-right side of the main gully, retracing the zigzag line back past the cave and reddish boulder, and back across the talus field to the Snowy Lakes camp. The gully is the crux of the descent from a hazard standpoint: the rock is loose and rockfall is a real risk both from your own party and from any other parties on route, so descend it deliberately, one person at a time through constrictions, and keep helmets on until clear of the gully and talus. From Snowy Lakes, reverse the approach hike out via Granite Pass and Cutthroat Pass back to the Rainy Pass PCT trailhead; if Granite Pass still holds snow, downclimb it with the same care (ice axe) used on the way in.
hazards: Loose, rockfall-prone rock in the main summit gully
Lingering snow/ice in the gully through June and sometimes into July
Afternoon thunderstorms common in summer with no shelter on the exposed ridge/gully
No cell service anywhere on the approach or climb

waysIn.name: Rainy Pass PCT over Cutthroat and Granite Passes to Snowy Lakes, then the reddish boulder and the cave
waysIn.season: Jul-Sep
waysIn.notes:
Start at the Rainy Pass PCT trailhead at about 4,875 ft on SR-20, 4.7 miles west of Washington Pass. Follow the Pacific Crest Trail northbound as it switchbacks up through forest and into larch parkland to Cutthroat Pass at about 6,800 ft, roughly 4.9 miles. This stretch has only intermittent small streams, so fill up at the last stream below the pass, which is itself dry; there is little reliable water again until Snowy Lakes.

From Cutthroat Pass the PCT contours below Cutthroat Peak's west flank to Granite Pass at about 6,300 ft, roughly 6.5-7 miles in. Granite Pass holds snow into July or August and when snow-covered is steep and exposed enough to warrant an ice axe. Beyond it the trail sidehills below Tower Mountain's west side, crosses a cliff-cut blasted-out section, loses a little elevation into a meadowed basin.

Roughly 9.5-10 miles in, about a mile before Methow Pass at about 6,300 ft, a climbers' use path branches right, east, off the PCT and climbs about half a mile and 400 ft to the Snowy Lakes basin, the standard base camp with reliable water and good tent sites.
hazards: A notoriously loose and rockfall-prone summit gully; climb one at a time through constrictions
Granite Pass holds snow into July or August and is steep and exposed when covered; carry an axe
Little reliable water between Cutthroat Pass and Snowy Lakes
A cliff-cut, blasted-out section of trail between Granite and Methow Passes
Roughly 10-11 miles one-way to camp before any climbing

name: North Couloir
approach: From the Cascade Pass Trailhead (end of Cascade River Road, ~23.1 mi from Marblemount), travel via Cascade Pass or the nearby Alliteration Col and descend/traverse east through the Pelton Basin area to Trapper Lake (el. ~4,170 ft), sitting just northeast of Trapper Mountain. From the lake, boot or skin directly to the base of the obvious north-facing couloir splitting the summit block, switching to crampons/ski (ascent) plates as the snow firms up higher on the route.
descent: The couloir is typically descended on skis/splitboard by the same line, managing sluff in the sustained 45-50 degree middle section; parties have encountered moats and debris (rock, fallen trees, ice chunks) piled at the base near Trapper Lake by early summer. From Trapper Lake, re-climb to Cascade Pass (or Alliteration Col) and follow the Cascade Pass Trail back to the trailhead; one documented car-to-car round trip took about 11.75 hours.
hazards: Wet-slide activity off slopes adjacent to Hurry-up Peak, reported as large as D2-3.
Rockfall potential from the couloir's walls.
Moats and inconsistent snow bridges near Trapper Lake.
Off-trail travel and creek crossings on the approach.

waysIn.name: Over the pass at the head of the river road, then east and down to the lake
waysIn.season: Spring into early summer, while the couloir still holds continuous snow
waysIn.notes:
From the trailhead at the end of the river road, climb to the pass at about 5,392 ft - or to the nearby col used as an alternative when the pass is corniced - and then travel east, descending and traversing through the basin beyond, to the lake at about 4,170 ft, which sits just north-east of the peak. From the lake you boot or skin directly to the foot of the route, changing to crampons or ascent plates as the snow firms up higher.

This is the approach that suits the route's season: the couloir is a snow line, so the party wants it early, which is also when the pass is a straightforward snow climb rather than a scramble.
hazards: a corniced pass early in the season, with an alternative col that carries its own hazards
a descent east from the pass that must be re-climbed at the end of the day
avalanche terrain in the couloir and the basin below it in spring
wet-snow release and rockfall out of the couloir once the sun reaches the face
a remote basin with a long retreat and no trail on the eastern side

waysIn.name: From the valley on the east, reaching the lake basin from below
waysIn.season: Summer, once the valley trail is open and the basin is snow-free enough to walk
waysIn.notes:
The lake basin can also be reached from the valley to the east, which is entered by boat or floatplane and then by road and trail up the valley floor. This is the approach the other route on this peak uses, and it puts a party at the lake without any pass to cross.

Treat the detail of it with caution. The published descriptions of this peak disagree about which drainage is followed off the valley trail and how far the lake is from the road, and the two accounts cannot both be right - so plan this variant from current maps and imagery rather than from a written description, and expect the off-trail section to be unmarked and steep.
hazards: an approach that depends on boat or floatplane schedules to reach the valley at all
an unmarked, steep off-trail push into the basin with no tread to follow out
conflicting written descriptions of which drainage is used, so navigate from maps rather than prose
avalanche terrain in the couloir in spring
a long committing distance from any road
waysIn.whyThisWay: When coming up from the Stehekin valley by boat instead of crossing the pass; the climb to the lake is off trail, steep and brushy, and the way is not marked.

name: South Slopes
approach: Start at the Cascade Pass Trailhead at the end of Cascade River Road and follow the maintained trail over Cascade Pass and down the Stehekin side to Pelton Basin. From the lowest tent sites at Pelton Basin, leave the trail on a faint boot path dropping toward Pelton Creek; below that the fisherman's path to Trapper Lake appears and vanishes, so expect route-finding through brush and alder before a flat, marshy walk along the inlet stream to the lake. Most parties treat this as a 2-3 day trip with a camp at Trapper Lake. The lake can also be reached by a steep off-trail climb from the upper Stehekin valley, but that line is harder to locate and first requires reaching Stehekin by boat or floatplane.
descent: Descend by reversing the south-slopes/basin ascent line back to Trapper Lake; no rappels are needed on the standard route. Loose talus and heather benches call for careful footing, especially late in the day when upper slopes have softened or afternoon thunderstorms are building.
hazards: Long off-trail approach with real route-finding/navigation risk
High, cold creek crossings during snowmelt (June-early July)
Loose talus and heather on the upper south slopes
No cell coverage and very little party traffic — self-rescue only
Afternoon thunderstorms common in late summer on this crest-adjacent peak

waysIn.name: Up the valley from the landing, then off-trail into the lake basin
waysIn.season: Midsummer through early autumn, once the basin is walkable and the valley road and trail are open
waysIn.notes:
There is no road to this side of the peak. Reach the valley by ferry or floatplane, then take the valley road or the park shuttle to a campground and pick up the valley trail from there. The lake below the peak is reached by leaving that trail and pushing off-trail and unmarked into the basin - a steep, poorly marked fisherman's path at best, and map-and-compass travel above it. Figure a full day of travel each way and plan on two or three days with a camp at or below the lake.

The off-trail departure is not well defined; plan it from current maps and imagery before you go.
hazards: reaching the valley at all depends on a ferry or floatplane and a shuttle
an unmarked off-trail push into the basin with no reliable path
loose unconsolidated talus and steep heather benches with unstable footing
no tread to follow on the descent, on ground where every slope looks the same
an exposed class 3 finish off the ridge
conflicting records of the approach drainage, so the departure point must be planned from maps
waysIn.whyThisWay: Midsummer, when the basin is walkable, for parties who would rather ride the ferry and shuttle than cross and recross the pass, accepting a longer, unmarked valley push.

waysIn.name: Over the pass at the head of the river road and down to the lake from the west
waysIn.season: Late spring into summer, while the pass is straightforward and the basin beyond is still simple travel
waysIn.notes:
The lake can also be reached from the other side of the range, by climbing to the pass at about 5,392 ft at the head of the river road - or the nearby col used when the pass is corniced - and then travelling east, descending and traversing through the basin beyond to the lake at about 4,170 ft.

This avoids the ferry and the unmarked valley push entirely, at the cost of a pass crossing in each direction and a descent that has to be re-climbed at the end of the trip.
hazards: a corniced pass in early season
a descent from the pass that must be re-climbed on the way out
loose talus and heather with unstable footing and no tread
an exposed class 3 finish
a basin with no path and no obvious exit seen from above

name: Traverse of Mount Index
approach: From the Lake Serene Trailhead, follow the maintained Lake Serene Trail #1068 roughly 4 miles and about 2,000 ft of gain to the lake basin. Traverse around the west side of the lake over talus and boulders to its south end, then climb steep brush and a gully system (snow-covered into early summer) toward the base of the North Peak's North Face. The standard North Face Route is a long, moderate alpine rock climb (Grade III, 5.6-5.7) on featured but sometimes rotten rock with significant brush; parties typically climb it car-to-car in a very long day (12-15+ hours) or with a bivy.
descent: Rappel from three peaks back down the route. Established anchors on traverse line use trees and bushes. Several 30-50 foot rappels; pack adequate sling material. Accomplish 2-3 hour descent from Main Peak to Lake Serene via rappels.
hazards: Persistent rockfall hazard, especially on exposed ridge sections
Very loose rock on all three peaks, particularly Middle and Main
Water scarcity in late season; snow/water in early season
Avalanche danger in early season with wet heavy snow
Severe route-finding challenges if visibility compromised
Mental fatigue from sustained climbing over 12+ hours

waysIn.name: Lake Serene Trail #1068 to the North Peak north face
waysIn.season: Jul-Aug for dry rock across all three summits
waysIn.notes:
US-2 at milepost 35.2, south on Mount Index Road 0.3 miles to the Lake Serene trailhead at about 600 ft. Lake Serene Trail #1068 runs about 4 miles and 2,000 ft to the lake basin; the maintained trail ends at the lake's north end.

Traverse the west side of the lake over talus and very large boulders to its south end, then climb steep brush and a gully system toward the base of North Peak's north face. That gully carries snow into early summer.

Budget headlamps in the morning to reach the lake so the technical section starts at first light: parties commonly need 12 to 15 hours or more, and many bivy.
hazards: Wet mossy slabs on the lower face
Steep brush with vertical steps and no protection
Rotten rock and sparse protection on the ridge between summits
Notches on the traverse needing careful downclimbing or short rappels
Very long committing day with poor escape options

name: Southwest Slopes / Lucky Pass
approach: Start at Colonial Creek Campground on SR-20 (Diablo Lake, milepost 130, roughly 25 miles east of Marblemount) and park in the large lot above the boat ramp on the campground's south side — this is also the Thunder Creek Trailhead. Follow the maintained Thunder Creek Trail south about 6.5-6.7 miles to McAllister Camp (~1,900 ft), a backcountry stock camp where McAllister Creek meets Thunder Creek. The trail's original bridge over Thunder Creek near mile 6.6 washed out in fall 2017; parties now cross on logs a short way upstream of the old bridge site. Across the creek, pick up the unmaintained climbers' boot path at the first fork, climbing steeply through brush and around downed timber up the north ridge; a viewpoint near 4,600 ft gives the first look at Primus, Tricouni, and neighboring peaks. Continue through forest and heather to Borealis Lake (base camp), a flat bench below the Borealis Glacier. From camp, rope up for glacier travel and climb the Borealis Glacier, skirting the icefall in its middle — it has retreated significantly and split into upper and lower tiers separated by slabs and cliffs — navigating crevasses to Lucky Pass, the Primus-Tricouni col. From Lucky Pass, climb a steep snow finger roughly 200 ft up Tricouni's southwest side, then transition to rock ramps and ledges (class 3-4 scrambling) up the west ridge to the bouldery 8,102 ft summit. Hazards: crevasses on the Borealis Glacier (worse late season), a brushy and poorly marked boot path above McAllister Camp, and afternoon softening of the snow finger. In late August, the Thunder Creek crossing near the old bridge site needed only a little wading, and a log near the log jam just upstream gave a way across on the return; earlier in summer the creek is deeper.
descent: Reverse the ascent: downclimb the rock ramps/ledges and snow finger back to Lucky Pass, then retrace the roped route across the Borealis Glacier to Borealis Lake camp. From camp, descend the boot path down the north ridge through brush and timber back to McAllister Camp, then follow the maintained Thunder Creek Trail out to Colonial Creek Campground — including the log crossing of Thunder Creek near mile 6.6 where the original bridge washed out in 2017. This is a walk-off/downclimb on snow, glacier, and class 3-4 rock; there is no rappelling and no fixed anchors on this route. Descent hazards mirror the approach (crevasses, brushy routefinding) plus afternoon sun softening the snow finger and Borealis Glacier into wet-slide/avalanche danger, so parties commonly start early to be off those slopes before they soften.
hazards: Crevasses on the Borealis Glacier — parties describe it as increasingly retreated, split into upper/lower tiers separated by slabs and cliffs, and harder to navigate as the ice retreats
Loose, blocky rock (Class 3-4) on the west ridge/summit
Brushy, unmaintained boot path above McAllister Camp with downed timber and limited route-finding cues
Afternoon thunderstorms in summer and softening of the snow finger/glacier surface
Long, remote self-rescue distance with no cell coverage

waysIn.name: Thunder Creek, Borealis Lake and Lucky Pass
waysIn.season: July and August are best; earlier ascents need ice technique, and the south-facing snow above the col softens dangerously through the day
waysIn.notes: From the large lot above the boat ramp at Colonial Creek, follow the maintained Thunder Creek Trail south to McAllister Camp; the old bridge near mile 6.6 is gone and the crossing is now on logs a short way upstream of the old site. Across the creek pick up the unmaintained boot path at the first fork, climbing steeply through brush and blowdown up the north ridge past a viewpoint that gives the first look at the peaks. Continue through forest and heather to the flat bench at Borealis Lake, the base camp. From camp rope up and climb the Borealis Glacier, skirting the icefall in its middle; it has retreated into an upper and a lower tier separated by slabs and cliffs, to the col.
hazards: Crevasses on the Borealis Glacier, worse late in the season
Brushy, poorly marked boot path above McAllister Camp
Afternoon softening of the south-facing snow finger — start early
Class 3-4 rock ramps and ledges above the snow

name: True Grit
approach: Start at the Sunrise Mine Trailhead (Sunrise Mine Trail #707) off the Mountain Loop Highway near Big Four/Barlow Pass. The trail begins in second-growth forest and almost immediately crosses the South Fork Stillaguamish via a log crossing that can be a genuine obstacle during high runoff (early season/after rain). From there the trail climbs steadily through Wirtz Basin, breaks out of the trees into open talus and boulder fields marked by cairns, and reaches Headlee Pass at roughly 4,720 ft and 2.7 miles in — a narrow, rocky notch/couloir with loose rock underfoot where rockfall from parties above is a real hazard. Past the pass the trail drops briefly through trees, then crosses about a third of a mile of talus to Vesper Creek, which it follows up to Vesper Lake (Lake Elan, ~4,950 ft, ~3.5 mi/~2,700 ft gain from the trailhead) — the last reliable running water before the climb. From the lake, cross the outlet and follow the summit trail up talus and slabs to roughly 5,600-5,700 ft, then swing north across the slabs to the saddle/col between Vesper and Wolf Peak. From the saddle, a ledge system cuts across Vesper's north face at roughly 5,800 ft, reached by walking out steep, exposed heather benches that get slick when wet and hold a steep snow slope into early-to-mid summer (ice axe and possibly crampons recommended for that window). The ledge leads to a small notch overlooking the Vesper Glacier remnant, near where True Grit's start is found. Allow 3+ hours from the trailhead to the base of the route. The two usual ways to the col notch near 5,720 ft are a traverse north from the trail at about 5,630 ft or a line hugging the west side of Lake Elan; going higher than that forces a slick slab down-climb to reach the col (August).
descent: True Grit tops out on Vesper's summit headwall/ridge, and the descent is a walk-off rather than a rappel-based exit — 0 rappels under normal conditions. From the top, downclimb/scramble class 3-4 terrain on the peak's southeast side; for most of the season this is a straightforward roughly 30-degree snow slope that can be glissaded or plunge-stepped (ice axe strongly recommended, crampons useful early season), while by late August/September the snow is gone and it's a walk down open slabs and talus instead. Aim for the Vesper-Wolf saddle, which is visible above Vesper Lake, then drop back to the lake outlet and pick up the talus ridge and Sunrise Mine Trail for the hike out. No technical anchors are needed; parties report the whole car-to-car outing (climb plus this descent) commonly taking 8-11 hours.
hazards: Loose rock from freeze-thaw and lichen, especially exiting P2's chimney
Early-season snow slope on the approach — an unprotected fall here would be serious
Runout sections above cliffs on the lower, easier pitches

waysIn.name: Sunrise Mine Trail #707, Headlee Pass, Vesper-Wolf saddle
waysIn.season: Jul-Sep; earlier needs axe and crampons for the ledge traverse
waysIn.notes:
Sunrise Mine trailhead off the Mountain Loop Highway via Sunrise Mine Road (FR 4065). Trail #707 crosses the South Fork Stillaguamish on a log almost immediately — a real obstacle in high runoff — then climbs through Wirtz Basin, breaks into cairned talus and boulder fields, and reaches Headlee Pass at about 4,720 ft and 2.7 miles. The pass is a narrow rocky notch with loose footing where rockfall from above is a genuine hazard.

Past the pass the trail drops briefly through trees, crosses about a third of a mile of talus to Vesper Creek and follows it up to Vesper Lake (Lake Elan) at about 4,950 ft, 3.5 miles and 2,700 ft from the car — last reliable water.

Stay on the ordinary Vesper summit trail up talus and slabs to roughly 5,600-5,700 ft, then leave it and swing north across the slabs. Three hours or more car to base.
hazards: Rockfall in the Headlee Pass couloir
Steep exposed heather benches, slick when wet
Snow on the ledge traverse into early-to-mid summer
Loose rock on the face — treat as alpine despite the bolted belays

name: East Slopes Scramble
approach: Park in the large day-use lot on the north side of US 2 right at the Stevens Pass summit (signed for the PCT/Skyline Lake trailhead); a Northwest Forest Pass or Forest Service day-use fee applies here. Leave from the lot beside the ski area's substation on the gated service road, and take the cairned left fork about a mile up to Skyline Lake and the gap in Skyline Ridge beyond it.
descent: Most parties descend the same east-slope line, watching footing carefully on loose talus and scree in the upper section. Some instead drop off the south ridge or the southeast-facing slopes back toward Skyline Ridge — scout the line before committing, since both options funnel into brush lower down. Lingering snow patches on shaded aspects can still be glissaded or plunge-stepped into early July.
hazards: No maintained trail — expect real route-finding through brush low on the route
Loose rock, talus, and scree on the upper slopes
Wind-exposed, unshaded summit ridge
Lingering snow/ice on shaded sections into early summer
No reliable water source above the trailhead

waysIn.name: Skyline Lake and the ridge gap drop-in
waysIn.season: Late June to October, or on snow
waysIn.notes: Start from the large day-use lot on the north side of the highway at the pass, beside the ski area's substation and utility building, on the gated service road. Around a mile in, an easy-to-miss cairn-marked left fork leaves the road for Skyline Lake and the ridge — staying right on the road takes you to a cell tower instead. Past the lake the route crosses the low point in Skyline Ridge, drops into a creek drainage on the ridge's back side, and climbs back out to gain the Tye Ridge crest. There is no maintained trail; snow-free this is a stiff bushwhack, which is why most ascents are made on continuous snow.
hazards: A roughly 150-ft slope near fifty degrees on the back side of the ridge gap, which can cornice in winter
Mossy, loose rock and brush on that drop-in when snow-free
Dense brush low on the route once the snow melts out
Loose talus and scree on the upper slopes
Wind-exposed summit ridge and no water above the creek drainage

name: Ultramega OK
approach: Start at the long highway pullout on SR-20 (~4,310 ft, near milepost 166, roughly 3.75 mi east of Washington Pass and directly across the valley from Silver Star Mountain). A boot path drops east through loose talus into forest; look for a registration box a few minutes in. The path fords Early Winters Creek on logs at about 4,080 ft (a swift wade in early season — trekking poles help). From the creek the trail climbs steadily east through forest and open slopes for roughly 2,200 ft to a broad flat bench/campsite around 6,460 ft, the approach's natural midpoint and a good high camp or bail point. Above the bench the boot path traverses loose scree gullies below Burgundy's northwest side and finishes up a final stretch of unstable, cairn-marked 'ball-bearing' scree over slab to Burgundy Col (~7,770–7,800 ft), the notch between Burgundy Spire and Paisano Pinnacle — about 3 miles and 3,500 ft one-way. From the col, Ultramega OK does not start at the col itself: scramble loose rock (or kick steps in lingering snow, ice axe recommended into July) down and around the base of Burgundy's north face until you reach a twin-crack system marked by obvious loose blocks about 60 ft up — this is the route start, climber's left of the North Face start, with Action Potential's clean splitter flake roughly 15 ft further left. Water is available at Early Winters Creek, a small trickle partway up near the col, and occasionally late-season ice on the col's east side. The loose final scree slopes below the col are the approach's main hazard — move carefully and stay bunched to avoid rockfall onto party members below.
descent: Ultramega OK has no independent, well-established rappel line of its own — it is a Northeast Buttress route whose last pitch finishes up an offwidth crack to the summit, though a party that loses the line high up can traverse ledges into upper North Face terrain (near Burgundy Ledge) and finish from there. From wherever the route is topped out, the standard way down is the North Face's 5-rappel descent: ~40m from a heavily slung summit boulder down the middle of the upper face to a bolted ledge anchor; ~55m from the bolts down lichen-covered rock to a huge ledge near a rock arch (traverse the ledge to a constriction with slings); ~55m from that constriction down to a blue-slung horn; ~40m from the horn to broad scree ledges (watch the rope pull here — lots of snag potential); and a final ~60m back to Burgundy Col. Double 60m ropes make this clean; parties with a single 70m have reported getting down with some downclimbing between stances, but it's tighter on this line than on the standard North Face. From the base of the raps, reverse the Burgundy Col approach back to the highway. A few parties describe instead downclimbing loose 3rd/4th-class terrain on Burgundy's east side back toward the col to avoid rappelling altogether, but this is opportunistic route-finding rather than an established descent, and is not recommended in the wet or for parties unfamiliar with the terrain.
hazards: loose blocks near the start, about 60 ft up P1
sparse protection on the P4 roof/corner crux
route-finding difficulty above pitch 7
long, committing approach to Burgundy Col

waysIn.name: The Wine Spires pullout and Burgundy Col, then further around the north face to the twin cracks with loose blocks
waysIn.season: Jul-Sep
waysIn.notes:
Start at the long highway pullout on SR-20 at about 4,310 ft near milepost 166, roughly 3.75 miles east of Washington Pass and directly across the valley from Silver Star Mountain. A boot path drops east through loose talus into forest; look for a registration box a few minutes in.

The path fords Early Winters Creek on logs at about 4,080 ft, a swift wade in early season. From the creek it climbs steadily east through forest and open slopes for roughly 2,200 ft to a broad flat bench and campsite around 6,460 ft, the approach's natural midpoint and a good high camp or bail point. Above the bench the boot path traverses loose scree gullies below Burgundy's northwest side and finishes up a final stretch of unstable, cairn-marked ball-bearing scree over slab to Burgundy Col at about 7,770-7,800 ft, the notch between Burgundy Spire and Paisano Pinnacle. About 3 miles and 3,500 ft one-way.
hazards: Unstable ball-bearing scree over slab below the col, with rockfall onto party members below
Lingering snow on the traverse around the north face, wanting an axe into July
No independent rappel line; the descent merges into another route's terrain
A single 70 m rope leaves the descent tight, with downclimbing between stances
A swift wade of Early Winters Creek in early season

name: Upper North Ridge w/Great Gendarme
approach: From I-90 Exit 85, take Highway 970 east 7 miles to Teanaway Road, then bear right onto North Fork Teanaway Road continuing 22.5 miles total. From trailhead: via Lake Ingalls and Stuart Pass to Goat Pass, then east across the Stuart Glacier to the North Ridge notch
descent: From the true summit, travel southeast on blocky 3rd/4th-class terrain toward the false summit, follow cairns down into the Cascadian Couloir snowfield, then descend extended 3rd-class scree/talus to Ingalls Creek. Sherpa Glacier or a Sherpa Pass glissade are faster early-season alternatives for parties returning to a north-side camp.
hazards: The gendarme-bypass gully (rappelling right/west at its base) is prone to rockfall on dirty rock and is not recommended; the upper mountain is almost always shaded and can be icy/cold on the crux pitches

waysIn.name: Goat Pass and the Stuart Glacier to the fourth-class gully and the notch
waysIn.season: Roughly Jul-Sep; earlier the gully to the notch holds snow and the glacier crossing is simpler, later it is bare and looser
waysIn.notes:
From the Esmeralda Basin trailhead at the end of the North Fork Teanaway Road, take the Ingalls Way trail over Ingalls Pass, past Ingalls Lake toward Stuart Pass, then the climbers' path onto the talus shoulder under Stuart's West Ridge and northwest to Goat Pass at about 7,600 ft.

From Goat Pass, traverse onto and across the Stuart Glacier rather than along beneath it, aiming for a fourth-class gully that runs up to the obvious notch in the North Ridge. This is the difference between this route and the complete ridge in one sentence: the complete-ridge party traverses east below the glacier to the toe, this party crosses the glacier and goes up.

The notch is a bivy: there are two good sites in it, which is why parties who intend to climb the upper ridge in a day from a high camp use it.

Published descriptions of this route are frank that the last of the navigation is yours — one of them says outright to take a topographic map and work it out. Treat that as a real warning rather than as rhetoric.
hazards: Crevasses on the Stuart Glacier crossing from Goat Pass
Loose rock in the fourth-class gully to the notch, with parties above
Knife-edge exposure on the ridge above the notch
Gendarme bypass gully is rockfall-prone on dirty rock and not recommended
Upper mountain is shaded and cold, icy on the crux pitches
Awkward retreat from the Gendarme's offwidth; navigation above the notch is on you

waysIn.name: Mountaineer Creek and the Stuart Glacier from the north
waysIn.notes: From the Stuart Lake trailhead, follow the trail up Mountaineer Creek, then leave it for the climbers' path into the basin below the Stuart and Sherpa glaciers. Climb the Stuart Glacier to the notch where the upper ridge begins. This suits parties camping in the north-side basin, but leaves the car on the opposite side from the Cascadian Couloir descent.
hazards: Stuart Glacier climbed to reach the notch; crevasse hazard on the glacier
Snow-filled gully to the ridge, usually climbed on fourth-class rock along its edge
Off-trail climbers' path from Mountaineer Creek into the basin below the Stuart and Sherpa glaciers
Knife-edge exposure on the ridge above the notch
Gendarme bypass gully is rockfall-prone on dirty rock and not recommended
Upper mountain is shaded and cold, icy on the crux pitches
No water on the ridge; bivy ledges are few and exposed
waysIn.whyThisWay: Early in the season, or for parties camping in the north-side basin, since it avoids the long Ingalls and Goat Pass hike; leaves the car opposite the usual descent.

name: Standard Route (Ares Tower)
approach: Park at the unsigned 'Wine Spires' pullout on SR-20, about 3.7 miles east of Washington Pass (roughly 0.7 mile past the Cutthroat Lake Road turnoff, near milepost 166), at about 4,300 ft elevation. A boot path drops down loose, scree-covered talus into the trees, passes a trail register, and crosses Early Winters Creek on logs at about 4,080 ft. The trail then climbs steadily through forest, steepening between two side creeks, gaining roughly 3,700+ ft to Burgundy Col (~7,800 ft); a flat bench campsite ('the Bench,' ~6,460 ft) sits about halfway up and is the more common camp for this objective. Vasiliki Ridge and Ares Tower rise directly north of Burgundy Col and the Wine Spires camp area; from the bench or col, contour and scramble north along the ridge crest to reach the base of Ares Tower.
descent: Rappel from the fixed anchor at the Ares Tower summit down to the notch to retrieve stashed gear, then reverse the 4th-class ridge scramble and descend the Burgundy Col approach trail back to Early Winters Creek and the SR-20 pullout.
hazards: Loose, scree-covered talus on the initial descent from the roadside pullout to Early Winters Creek
Early-season crossing of Early Winters Creek on logs can be swift and high with snowmelt
Rockfall on the ridge, especially with other parties above or in unsettled weather
Afternoon thunderstorms are common on the exposed ridge crest in summer
Route-finding: Vasiliki Tower, The Acropolis, and Niki Tower are similar granite towers on the same ridge crest and are easy to mistake for Ares Tower, the true high point

waysIn.name: The Wine Spires pullout to the Bench, then north along the ridge crest to Ares Tower
waysIn.season: Jun-Sep
waysIn.notes:
Park at the unsigned Wine Spires pullout on SR-20, about 3.7 miles east of Washington Pass, roughly 0.7 mile past the Cutthroat Lake Road turnoff near milepost 166, at about 4,300 ft. A boot path drops down loose scree-covered talus into the trees, passes a trail register, and crosses Early Winters Creek on logs at about 4,080 ft.

The trail then climbs steadily through forest, steepening between two side creeks, gaining roughly 3,700-plus ft to Burgundy Col at about 7,800 ft. A flat bench campsite, the Bench, at about 6,460 ft sits about halfway up and is the more common camp for this objective than the col itself.
hazards: A class 4 ridge traverse with real exposure to reach the tower
Loose scree-covered talus on the initial drop from the highway
A log crossing of Early Winters Creek
The whole approach shares a trail with the Wine Spires objectives and then deliberately departs from it

name: Standard Route (Headlee Pass)
approach: From the Sunrise Mine trailhead, Trail 707 crosses several streams in the first mile, including the main South Fork Stillaguamish, which has no bridge and can be a serious obstacle when runoff is high. The trail then climbs through forest and an open talus basin before tightening into steep, narrow switchbacks up the couloir to Headlee Pass, about 2.7 miles from the trailhead. From the pass, the trail traverses the south flank of Sperry Peak into the upper Vesper Creek basin, where the route leaves the lake trail at the creek crossing.
descent: Descend the same way. Take care to find the central rib again on the slabs, since the gullies to the descender's right lead into steeper ground, and go slowly down the loose Headlee Pass couloir.
hazards: The South Fork Stillaguamish crossing has no bridge and can be dangerous in high runoff.
Rockfall in the narrow Headlee Pass couloir, often knocked down by other parties above.
Falls of 10-20 feet are possible on the upper slabs.
Steep, exposed terrain on the east side of the summit block.
A steep snowfield can linger near the summit into summer.

name: Southeast Peak Standard (Home Lake approach)
approach: Drive Highway 101 to Sequim Bay State Park area, turn left on Louella Road for 1 mile, then left on Palo Alto Road for about 5.8 miles (it becomes FS Road 28 at the Forest Boundary), then turn right onto FS Road 2880, drive past Dungeness Forks Campground for 1 mile, stay left onto FS Road 2870 for 8.7 miles to Upper Dungeness Trailhead. Upper Dungeness Trail is the shortest and easiest approach. Hike the trail 3.4 miles and 600 feet to Camp Handy, then take the left fork and continue 3 miles and 1,850 feet to Boulder Camp (total: 6.4 miles, 2,450 feet gain). From Boulder Camp, continue south approximately 1.5-2 miles, crossing creeks, until you reach the final larger creek that flows from the cirque SE of Warrior Peak. Continue past this creek to a boulder field, then head up and back left toward the creek, staying under a band of cliffs, and continue up the boulders approximately 1 mile and 1,200 feet to reach the cirque at approximately 5,900 feet.
descent: Reverse the route: downclimb or carefully descend the crux rock step back to the ~7,000 ft saddle, then descend the couloir and cirque back toward Home Lake. Parties describe the snow chute descent as fast and consequential if glissaded without a clear view of the runout — at least one party described nearly going over a cliff band while glissading nearby terrain, and rockfall in the gully is a recurring hazard, so keep parties spread out and avoid glissading unless the full runout is visible and safe.
hazards: Loose, poor-quality rock on the final headwall above the 7,000 ft saddle — a recurring theme across trip reports.
Rockfall in the summit couloir/gully between the twin summits, especially with parties above or after freeze-thaw cycles.
Glissade/uncontrolled-slide risk descending the snow chute if the runout isn't fully visible.
Faint, use-trail-only route-finding above Home Lake through forest, meadow, and talus.
Fast-moving Pacific frontal systems and late-summer afternoon thunderstorms typical of the Olympics.

waysIn.name: Upper Dungeness Trail, Camp Handy and Boulder Shelter to the southeast cirque
waysIn.season: Roughly Jul-Sep. Snow in the summit couloir into early season is an improvement on the scree that replaces it
waysIn.notes:
From US-101 near Sequim Bay State Park turn on Louella Road for a mile, then Palo Alto Road for about 5.8 miles, becoming FS Road 28 at the forest boundary. Right on FS 2880 past Dungeness Forks Campground, then left on FS 2870 for 8.7 miles to the Upper Dungeness Trailhead. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass required at the kiosk.

Trail #833.2 is the shortest and easiest approach. Hike 3.2-3.4 miles and about 600 ft to Camp Handy at roughly 3,100 ft, a riverfront meadow with a cedar-shingle shelter, then take the uphill fork and continue about 3 miles and 1,850 ft to Boulder Camp / Boulder Shelter at 6.3-6.4 miles and roughly 4,890-4,950 ft. The creek there is the most reliable water on the approach.

From Boulder Shelter hike south on the Dungeness / Constance Pass trail, crossing several creeks, toward Home Lake.
hazards: Loose, poor-quality rock on the final headwall above the 7,000 ft saddle — a recurring theme in every account
Rockfall in the couloir between the twin summits, worst with parties above or after freeze-thaw
Glissade and uncontrolled-slide risk descending the snow chute if the runout is not fully visible — one party described nearly going over a cliff band on nearby terrain
Faint use-trail-only route-finding above the trail through forest, meadow and talus
Fast-moving Pacific frontal systems and late-summer afternoon thunderstorms

waysIn.name: Home Lake basecamp, from either the Dungeness or the Dosewallips side
waysIn.season: Roughly Jul-Sep
waysIn.notes:
Home Lake at about 5,308-5,330 ft, walled in by Mount Constance and Warrior Peak just below Constance Pass, is the standard basecamp for this climb and it is reachable from two directions: north up the Upper Dungeness / Constance Pass trail at roughly 9.3 miles from the Upper Dungeness Trailhead, or south from the Dosewallips road end over Constance Pass. An Olympic National Park wilderness permit is required.

Camping at Home Lake rather than pushing from Boulder Shelter turns this into a comfortable two-day trip and puts you a mile from the cirque. It is also the camp shared with Mount Fricaba, Mount Mystery and Mount Deception parties, so it is well-used ground with an established site.

From the lake, leave the basin and climb east into the Warrior / Inner Constance cirque through meadow and talus.
hazards: Same as the Boulder Shelter variant: loose summit rock, couloir rockfall, glissade runout, faint route-finding
Home Lake sits below Constance Pass, so an exit north regains meaningful height before the long descent
Wilderness permit required and the site is popular with parties climbing four different peaks
waysIn.whyThisWay: When you want a relaxed two-day trip with a camp a mile from the cirque, or you are linking the neighbouring peaks from the same lake; the Dosewallips side is longer and rarely used.

name: Standard Route (South Ridge / South Gully via Copper Glance Basin)
approach: From Winthrop, drive north about 8 miles on West Chewuch Road (County Road 1213) to Eightmile Road (Forest Road 5130), then continue roughly 12-15 miles northwest along Eightmile Creek to the Copper Glance Trailhead (about 3,800-3,810 ft; no fee). Hike Copper Glance Trail #519, which begins on an old mining-claim jeep track/tramway grade (FSR 505) for about 1.5 miles to the historic Copper Glance mine, crosses Copper Glance Creek (the creek's bridge has been reported washed out or missing in some years, requiring a ford), and continues through a 2018 burn area past a small pond to Copper Glance Lake and the open upper basin below Isabella Ridge (about 3.3-3.5 miles one-way, ~6,260-6,600 ft) — a common camp/base for the peak.
descent: From the summit, downclimb the south ridge back into the gully/chute and descend the loose scree and talus to the upper basin. Where snow remains, an ice axe (and crampons/microspikes if firm) is useful, and glissading the snow sections can speed descent when conditions allow. Below the basin, retrace the Copper Glance Trail past the mine site and back down the old tramway grade to the trailhead, re-fording Copper Glance Creek where the bridge is out.
hazards: Sustained loose talus and scree with real rockfall potential on the ascent/descent gully
Residual steep snow in the couloir/gully into early-mid summer, requiring an ice axe
Cornices and avalanche-prone terrain if attempted in winter or spring
High-water creek crossing at Copper Glance Creek in early season

waysIn.name: Copper Glance Basin and the south-side chute
waysIn.season: July to September
waysIn.notes: West Craggy is the lower of the two Craggy summits and is normally climbed on the same trip as its neighbour, the two being joined by a saddle. The approach is short by the standards of this country: a forest road reaches the trailhead and the Copper Glance trail reaches the open basin in a few miles, starting on an old mining jeep track, passing the mine ruins, crossing the creek where the bridge has been out in various years, and running through burn to the lake and the basin above it. A knoll at about 6,600 ft in the basin is the usual camp. The climbing is class 2 with occasional short scrambling, and the two real considerations are loose rock and how much snow is left in the gully.
hazards: Sustained loose talus and scree with real rockfall potential in the gully
Steep residual snow in the chute into early or mid summer
Cornices and avalanche terrain if attempted in winter or spring
High water at the Copper Glance Creek crossing in early season
No water above the basin crossing
Class 3 downclimbing with exposure if the direct descent line is taken

name: West Ridge
approach: Follow the shared Wine Spires trail: boot path down talus to Early Winters Creek, cross on a log, then climb steeply up the timbered rib north of Burgundy Creek to the ~6,500 ft basin/camp (roughly 2 hours from the car). Paisano Pinnacle's West Ridge route starts lower than Burgundy Spire's and is commonly linked with Burgundy Spire's North Face in one long car-to-car day; fresh water is reported from a spring near the camp bench.
descent: From the summit, downclimb easier terrain for a few hundred feet, then make two rappels — 30m and 20m — down into the gully beneath Burgundy Col, downclimbing sections between the rappel anchors. From the gully, follow the climbers' trail back down past the bench camp, cross Early Winters Creek, and finish with a short climb back up to the highway pullout.
hazards: Sparsely protected, runout summit slab pitch.
Loose rock on the approach rib and descent gully.
Standard alpine rockfall and afternoon-thunderstorm exposure at ~7,900 ft.

waysIn.name: Unsigned highway pullout east of Washington Pass, the timbered rib to the bench, then the contour right
waysIn.season: Roughly June through September; the approach holds snow into June and access disappears when the highway closes
waysIn.notes:
Park in the broad unsigned pullout on the highway about four miles east of Washington Pass, at roughly 4,250 to 4,300 ft. It is signed for the mountain above rather than for the spires, and nothing marks the climbers' path.

The path drops down the talus and into the forest, crosses Early Winters Creek on a log, and then climbs steeply up the timbered rib on the left — the north side — of the creek that drains the col above. Two hours or so of steep walking puts you on the basin bench at about 6,500 ft. There is a spring near the bench camp and it is the last reliable water.

From the bench the trail continues another three-quarters of an hour to the col at about 7,720 ft, which is the hub for the whole cluster. This route does not need to go that far.

The pullout doubles as the overnight for most parties. Nothing there is developed — no toilet, no table, no water — and highway noise carries.
hazards: Unsigned pullout and unmarked climbers' path with no trail signs anywhere
The start is a single jammed block; the lower ridge offers several plausible wrong starts
The final pitch is runout exposed face climbing with marginal protection
Rope drag on the long crest pitch if slings are not managed
Early Winters Creek is crossed on a log and is worse in high water

name: South Route
approach: Start at the Goodell Creek Cross-Country Zone trailhead off SR-20 just west of Newhalem (this is the drive-in endpoint). From the trailhead, follow the climbers' path up the old, overgrown Goodell Creek logging-road corridor through open forest for roughly 3.5 miles; beyond the fork where the maintained tread ends, the route becomes a boot path through talus with only sparse flagging, so follow cairns rather than a continuous trail. This talus/boulder-hopping stretch leads to a crossing of Terror Creek — look for a cairn marking the ford; water levels are seasonal and the crossing can go from a rock-hop in late season to a genuinely wet, current-fed ford in early summer or after rain. Beyond the creek, the route climbs a steep, brushy rib known informally as 'the Barrier': tree debris, slide alder, and a faded, easy-to-lose boot path make this the route-finding crux of the approach. Water becomes scarce above about 5400 ft — expect only dry streambeds and the occasional small puddle, so treat any water below the Barrier as your last reliable fill-up. The path tops out and drops about 200 ft into Crescent Creek Basin, then traverses roughly a mile north across scree to the common Southern Pickets camp below Mount Terror at about 6050 ft, fed by two streams coming off the slabs above (reliable water and the standard base camp for this side of the range). From camp, West Twin Needle's south side presents two gullies right of a dividing buttress; the true line follows a minor rib on climber's left of the rightmost gully (which cliffs out in a closed chimney) up to a notch at about 7400 ft below the Eye Col, the gap between the two Twin Needles. The technical crux of the approach is pitching through this 'Eye Col' gully past large chockstones on low 5th-class rock, including one narrow-crack pitch typically taken on a belay. From the notch, easy slabs and scrambling (roughly 5.7) lead to the summit. Total round trip from the trailhead runs about 19.5 miles (~31 km) with well over 7000 ft of gain. Expect loose rock throughout the gullies, sustained route-finding through brush and scree, exposed scrambling on the connecting ribs, and unreliable water above the Barrier.
descent: Rather than reversing the ascent gully to the Eye Col, descend the class 2–3 west face to the Himmelhorn–West Twin Needle notch on the far side of the peak. Below that, plan on 2 rappels using doubled 60m ropes to get past a band of vertical slabs — parties report the first anchor built on a protruding rock angled upward (to keep a rappel sling from walking off) and a second anchor set above boulders in the south gully; treat these as natural/gear anchors rather than fixed bolted stations; bring cord/rap rings since existing tat should not be counted on. From the base of the rappels, grassy benches sit around 6800 ft; from there traverse east and climb back up roughly 200 ft to regain the 'left gully,' which is then downclimbed/scrambled to the base near the buttress that splits the approach gullies. From there, retrace the south-route approach line back down through Crescent Creek Basin to camp. Where conditions and the exact line allow, some parties instead reverse the east-face gully (class 2–3) directly into Crescent Creek Basin, avoiding the technical col rappels entirely but at the cost of more sustained loose, exposed scrambling — this is the non-technical walk-off alternative referenced in older route notes. Watch for loose blocks throughout and be prepared for stuck ropes on retrieval (reported by at least one party, freed with a hard tug) — a real risk on this kind of low-angle-slab rappel line.
hazards: Loose, friable rock typical of the Southern Pickets - a 2009 rockfall accident on nearby Mount Terror's Stoddard Buttress (a large 'solid-looking' block that tore loose) illustrates the risk on similar terrain
Rockfall in the narrow approach/route gullies, especially with other parties above
Reportedly disorienting route-finding in the basin and lower gully system
Water scarcity on the Barrier approach ridge in late-season conditions
Remote location - any serious injury likely requires helicopter evacuation given the multi-day approach and unreliable cell coverage

waysIn.name: Crescent Creek Basin camp to the Eye Col gully
waysIn.season: Mid-July to September, once the basin and the gully system are melted out
waysIn.notes: From the Goodell Creek trailhead follow the climbers' path up the old overgrown logging-road corridor; beyond the fork where the maintained tread ends it becomes a boot path through talus with sparse flagging, so follow cairns. Cross Terror Creek at the cairned ford — a rock-hop late in the season and a genuine wet crossing in early summer — then climb the steep brushy rib known as the Barrier, which is the route-finding crux of the walk in. The path tops out and drops a couple of hundred feet into Crescent Creek Basin, then traverses north across scree to the standard camp fed by two streams off the slabs above. Water is scarce above about 5,400 ft, so treat the last of it below the Barrier as your fill-up.
hazards: Loose rock throughout the gullies
Sustained route-finding through brush and scree with an easy-to-lose boot path on the Barrier
Unreliable water above the Barrier
Chockstone pitches at the col on low fifth-class rock, including one narrow crack normally belayed

name: Western Dihedral
approach: South Face is the southwest-facing slab wall around the corner west of the Illusion Wall, with its own approach separate from Waterfall Basin. Take I-5 to the Arlington exit, SR 530 east through Oso to Darrington, then Squire Creek Road to the washout-blocked parking area. Walk the old roadbed past the flagged landslide crossing to the brown Squire Creek Trail #654 sign and 8-10 minutes beyond it, to two cut logs either side of the road with old logging cable visible. Turn right a few steps past them on a well-beaten boot track, drop to Squire Creek and ford it where it is shallowest (hard in early season or after storms), then follow the climbers' track briefly downstream before it turns uphill, crosses a tributary and climbs old-growth forest and two gullies, steep and dirty near the top, to the grassy saddle, about 3 hours from the car. For this route go left (west) from the saddle to the base of Skeena26, scramble about 100 m of class 4 ramps and small dihedrals to a large shelf, follow it left to a deep gully (two-bolt anchor for a hand line or a short rappel), cross it and follow a cairned boot track west across talus and cedar ribs to the large talus field below the far western wall, about an hour from Skeena26.
descent: Descend by rappelling the line of ascent using the fixed hand-drilled bolt anchors; two 60m ropes recommended.
hazards: Steep, brushy, poorly maintained approach trail with stream crossings and old avalanche/rockslide debris
Remote location extends any self-rescue or evacuation timeline

waysIn.name: Squire Creek trail, cut logs, ford and the grassy saddle
waysIn.season: Summer
waysIn.notes:
From Darrington take Squire Creek Road to the washout that gates it, then walk the old roadbed past the flagged landslide crossing.

The South Face turn-off is two cut logs, one either side of the road, with old logging cable visible — turn right there onto the well-beaten boot track. It drops to a ford of the creek, then climbs steeply through old growth, steep and dirty near the top, into open grassland. The main grassy saddle bivy is about three hours from the trailhead, with a second smaller saddle roughly ten minutes further west along the wall.
hazards: Ford of Squire Creek
Steep dirty forest on the upper boot track
Hand-drilled bolts of unknown age on the face sections

name: South Ridge / Southwest Slope
approach: Two trailheads serve this scramble, both off SR-20 between Rainy Pass and Washington Pass. Option A (PCT approach, most commonly used): park at the marked Pacific Crest Trail North trailhead lot on the north side of Rainy Pass (~4,850 ft, next to the Road 600 turnoff). From the lot, leave the PCT almost immediately and strike out cross-country/climber's-path east into open forest, gaining steeply through timber and over downed logs — there is no maintained tread once you leave the PCT. Continue up through the trees (expect lingering snow patches into early summer) to about 6,100 ft, where the forest opens into a meadow basin below the west ridge/gully complex. From the basin, trend south/southeast on a rising traverse to gain the col/basin between Whistler and the southwest peak of Cutthroat, then work up the broad west ridge or the shallow gully just north of it to the summit shoulder; the final short section involves a rock gully with a visible ramp along the headwall over downsloping slabs and loose gravel — a helmet is recommended here for rockfall from parties above. Round trip via this line runs roughly 3.7 miles with about 3,000 ft of gain (trailhead 4,850 ft to summit 7,790 ft). Option B (highway turnout approach, reaches the true south ridge): from the unmarked pullout on SR-20 about 3.1 miles east of Rainy Pass (0.7 mile before the Blue Lake trailhead, ~5,000 ft), walk back down/along the road shoulder to a boot path that starts at the west edge of a stand of trees. Follow the boot path up through a meadow, then rising-traverse to intersect the level portion of Whistler's south ridge at about 6,180 ft. From there, scramble up the ridge and connecting gullies to the summit; alternatively leave the ridge around 6,800 ft, cross a couple of gullies left (west) onto gentler southwest-facing slopes, and finish to the summit that way. This line is also about 4 miles round trip with ~3,000 ft gain. Both approaches are trail-less above the first stretch of forest — expect route-finding, loose talus/scree in the gullies, and class 2-3 terrain with occasional class 3-4 moves and real exposure near the ridge crest and summit gully; no reliable water source above the lower forest, so carry what you need from the car. No creek fords or avalanche paths of note on the standard summer line, but early-season snow lingers in the forest and basin and can make the gully sections firm or icy. Crossing over to the stream too high in the forest costs extra bushwhacking; contour at a lower elevation instead.
descent: There is no rappelling on this route — it's a walk-off/downclimb, reversing whichever line was used on the way up. From the summit, downclimb the summit gully (loose gravel and downsloping slabs — take care with rockfall for anyone below) back to the shoulder, then descend either the west ridge/gully back into the meadow basin and forest (Option A) or drop onto the south ridge and retrace the rising traverse back to the meadow and boot path to the highway turnout (Option B). Loose rock and talus in the gullies is the main descent hazard — down-climb facing in on the steeper class 3 sections and stay alert for parties below. Some ski mountaineers descend a separate snow-filled west gully (~35°, over 1,000 ft of sustained fall-line terrain funneling to a waterfall lower down, requiring an exit right into the glades to avoid the falls) as a spring ski descent, but that is a snow-season variant, not part of the standard summer scramble descent, and should not be used as a hiking descent once snow is out. rappels: 0.
hazards: Wet-slab and cornice avalanche danger in the gullies during spring snow season
Loose talus, scree, and some loose rock in the summit gullies
Seasonal waterfall/creek crossing at the base of the west gully descent line
Afternoon thunderstorms common on the exposed ridge in summer
No reliable cell coverage in the Rainy Pass/Washington Pass corridor

waysIn.name: Rainy Pass PCT lot, then cross-country east into the meadow basin and the col toward Cutthroat's southwest peak
waysIn.season: Jul-Oct
waysIn.notes:
Park at the marked Pacific Crest Trail North trailhead lot on the north side of Rainy Pass at about 4,850 ft, next to the Road 600 turnoff. Leave the PCT almost immediately and strike out cross-country east into open forest, gaining steeply through timber and over downed logs. There is no maintained tread once you leave the PCT.

This is Whistler Mountain above Rainy Pass in Chelan County, not the Whistler Canyon trailhead area near Oroville, which is about 100 miles away and unrelated.

Round trip runs roughly 3.7 miles with about 3,000 ft of gain.
hazards: No maintained tread above the PCT; steep cross-country through timber and over downed logs
Rock gully with downsloping slabs and loose gravel near the summit, rockfall from parties above
Loose talus and scree in the gullies with class 3-4 moves and exposure near the crest
Lingering snow in forest and basin firms or ices the gullies early season
Wet-slab and cornice avalanche danger in the gullies in spring snow season
No reliable water above the lower forest
Afternoon thunderstorms on the exposed ridge

waysIn.name: The unmarked SR-20 turnout, then a boot path onto the true south ridge at 6,180 ft
waysIn.season: Jul-Oct
waysIn.notes:
The second option, and the one that reaches the true south ridge. From the unmarked pullout on SR-20 about 3.1 miles east of Rainy Pass, 0.7 mile before the Blue Lake trailhead, at about 5,000 ft, walk back down and along the road shoulder to a boot path that starts at the west edge of a stand of trees.

About 4 miles round trip with roughly 3,000 ft of gain, the same as the PCT option.
hazards: Unmarked pullout on SR-20 found only by distance from the Blue Lake trailhead; walk along the road shoulder
Trail-less above the first stretch of forest
Class 2-3 with occasional class 3-4 moves and real exposure near the ridge crest
Loose talus and scree in the connecting gullies
Wet-slab and cornice avalanche danger in the gullies in spring snow season
No reliable water on the route
Afternoon thunderstorms on the exposed ridge
waysIn.whyThisWay: When you want a boot path that reaches the true south ridge rather than cross-country timber from the PCT lot; it is about the same gain and a touch longer.

name: White Mountain Scramble
approach: Dosewallips approach (north): from the vehicle road end on the Dosewallips Road (about 8.5 mi from US-101), hike or bike the closed roadbed ~6.5-7 mi (~1,900 ft gain) to the former Dosewallips Ranger Station, then continue on the West Fork Dosewallips Trail to Honeymoon Meadows camp (about 14 miles from the road end, established campsite). Total approach gain to camp is roughly 5,300 ft. Duckabush approach (south/west): from the Duckabush River trailhead (Brinnon, drivable year-round, no washout), hike the Duckabush River Trail 6.2 mi to the park boundary and on toward O'Neil Pass (16.1 mi park-boundary-to-pass), camping at Marmot Lake (established site, toilet, bear wire), or continuing up past Hart Lake to Lake La Crosse in the basin directly below the peak.
descent: Standard descent is to reverse the ascent scramble route back to camp (Honeymoon Meadows or Marmot Lake depending on approach). There is no established rappel or technical descent; the main concerns are loose talus/scree on the upper slopes and losing the line back to camp in open forest/heather terrain with no marked path - note landmarks or track your ascent on the way up.
hazards: Remnant/unnamed glacier and permanent snowfield in the north cirque between White Mountain and Mount La Crosse - crevasse and steep-snow hazard in that terrain, especially early season
Faint, brushy, alder-choked tread on the LaCrosse Pass Trail near the Duckabush side - route-finding hazard, not a groomed trail
Unbridged stream/river crossings on the Duckabush and Dosewallips approaches that can be hazardous during high water or after storms
Loose talus and scree on the summit scramble slopes
Rapidly changing mountain weather and low cloud/whiteout on the open upper terrain
Long, remote multi-day approach with no cell coverage - limited options for self-rescue

waysIn.name: West Fork Dosewallips to Anderson Pass
waysIn.season: Mid-July to September; snow into July
waysIn.notes: The mountain is easy and the getting there is not. From the Dosewallips road end, the abandoned roadbed runs five and a half to seven miles up to the old ranger station, walked or ridden, then the West Fork trail carries on to the Honeymoon Meadows camp at roughly mile fifteen. Most parties sleep there and take the summit as a day out and back of about eight miles, climbing to Anderson Pass and leaving the trail. Water is reliable in the valley and effectively absent once you leave the pass, so fill up low. There is no tread, no cairn line and no marked path above the pass — carry a track or take bearings on the way up, because open forest and heather all look the same coming down in flat light.
hazards: A remnant glacier and permanent snowfield fill the north cirque between this summit and its higher neighbour — crevasse and steep-snow ground, worst early season
Loose talus and scree on the upper slopes
Unbridged crossings on both the Dosewallips and Duckabush approaches, serious in high water
No maintained path above camp, so a whiteout on the open upper terrain leaves nothing to follow
Multi-day remoteness with no cell coverage and slow self-rescue

name: Northwest Shoulder
approach: Drive Old Mine Road to its dead end at a steel gate (about 540 ft); the Niederprum Trailhead (Trail #653, ~918 ft) is about 1.25 miles farther up the old road on foot. Because the Moose Creek bridge just past the gate has been closed and barricaded with boulders for years, you now park at the gate, scramble over the boulder barricade, and cross the old wooden bridge on foot to rejoin the road to the actual trailhead about 1.25 miles farther on — this detour adds roughly 2.6 miles round trip and 400 ft of extra gain beyond what older published mileages state. From the signed trailhead, Trail #653 switchbacks up through forest for about 1.3 miles, crossing into Boulder River Wilderness (marked by a small boundary sign) and passing an old slide-alder opening with views north to Darrington and the Sauk Valley. At roughly 3,200 ft you reach 'the flat,' a level clearing that was the site of Chas Niederprum's old mining cabin — a natural rest/camp spot with good views of the peak. Beyond the flat the maintained tread ends; continue on a climbers' boot path through thinning, brushy forest (deadfall to weave around) up to continuous snow around 2,600 ft of gain from the trailhead. From there make a gently rising traverse south for about 0.5 mile into a wide, usually snow-filled couloir (holds snow into early July in normal years); ascend it to Lone Tree Pass (~4,970–5,000 ft, roughly 2 miles and 4,000+ ft above the trailhead — despite the name there are three trees near the pass, not one). From the pass, do a pleasant ridge traverse east for 600–700 m, then drop southeast through trees to a bench near a small lake/flat meadow (a sheltered, view-blessed bivy option). Continue a long rising traverse east for roughly 2 km through forest and open slopes below cliff bands, then climb a gully/open slope to High Pass (~6,032–6,100 ft). Cross High Pass onto the So-Bahli-Ahli (Whitehorse) Glacier and continue up snow (up to ~35° at the steepest) toward the summit snow ridge; rope up for crevasse hazard, which becomes real from roughly July onward. Key hazards along the way: the barricaded creek/bridge crossing at the start, avalanche-prone terrain in the entry couloir to Lone Tree Pass, vague/brushy route-finding beyond 'the flat,' crevasses on the upper glacier in mid-to-late season, and the summit bergschrund/moat, which by midsummer often forces a short section of 5th-class rock or a delicate roped snow-bridge crossing just below the top. No reliable water past the trailhead area once you're on snow — carry what you need or plan to melt.
descent: Descend by reversing the ascent line. From the true summit, downclimb the steep upper snow/ice slope below the top (up to about 60°, and often icy rather than soft by afternoon) back down to the bergschrund/moat that guards the summit block. Most parties make one rappel here to bypass the schrund rather than downclimb through it — anchor options are natural: slung webbing around a rock horn/chockstone, or an old fixed piton left by previous parties (treat any in-place tat or pins as suspect; one recent trip report had a piton fail under load, so back it up or build your own gear anchor in the rock). A doubled 30 m rope (or a single 60 m rope doubled) is generally sufficient to clear the gap; in lean/late-season years when the schrund has opened wider, some parties report needing two rappels or a longer single line.
