Early in the season, when the moat is well snow-bridged, this step can sometimes be downclimbed with a boot-axe belay instead. Below the schrund, re-cross the glacier, downclimb (or glissade, snow conditions permitting) back through the connecting slopes to High Pass, reverse the long traverse to Lone Tree Pass, then descend the entry couloir — a fast glissade or boot-ski in soft afternoon snow, a careful plunge-step descent if firm — back to treeline and the Niederprum Trail. From there it's a straightforward hike out to the trailhead and the Moose Creek bridge/boulder-barricade crossing. This is a long day: parties commonly report 12–14 hours car-to-car, so plan for an early alpine start and be off the upper glacier and past the couloir before afternoon warming increases rockfall/wet-slide risk.
hazards: Steep, brushy, sometimes muddy way-trail beyond the maintained tread
Loose rock in the gully above Lone Tree Pass
Crevasses opening on the So-Bahli-Ahli Glacier from July onward
Bergschrund/moat below the summit block — the technical crux, sometimes requiring a belayed crossing
Afternoon wet-slide and rockfall as the couloir and glacier warm
Exposed Class 3-4 downclimbing on tired legs late in a long day

waysIn.name: Niederprum Trail #653 to Lone Tree Pass and High Pass
waysIn.season: late Apr-Jun for snow cover; the line goes later but on more rock
waysIn.notes:
Niederprum trailhead at the end of Old Mine Road above Darrington. The Moose Creek bridge just past the gate has been closed and barricaded for years, so parties park at the gate, get past the barricade on foot and walk the road roughly a mile and a quarter to the real trailhead — extra distance and gain that older published figures do not include.

Trail #653 switchbacks through forest into the Boulder River Wilderness and reaches 'the flat' at about 3,200 ft, a level clearing on the site of an old mining cabin and the natural rest or camp spot. Beyond it the maintained tread ends and a boot path threads thinning, brushy forest with deadfall.

Above that the route traverses south through moderately dense forest between roughly 4,500 and 4,700 ft to reach a broad snow couloir, which is climbed to Lone Tree Pass at about 5,000 ft. From the pass, traverse east along the ridge and then drop several hundred feet southeast to a small lake and flat meadow — a sheltered bivy. A long rising traverse east below cliff bands then leads to a broad gully up to High Pass at about 6,100 ft, and over it onto the So-Bahli-Ahli (Whitehorse) Glacier.
hazards: barricaded Moose Creek bridge at the start
avalanche terrain in the entry couloir to Lone Tree Pass
vague, brushy route-finding with deadfall above 'the flat'
crevasses on the Whitehorse Glacier from roughly July onward
summit bergschrund and moat, often a fifth-class or roped step by midsummer
no reliable water once you are on snow

waysIn.name: Snow Gulch direct (deep snow only)
waysIn.season: early season, deep snow burying the brush
waysIn.notes: A more direct line used by some early-season and ski parties. From the Niederprum trailhead area, follow the old forest-road grade toward Snow Gulch, then ascend the creek drainage. The section between roughly 1,100 and 2,200 ft is a steep bushwhack through slide alder or up the adjacent slabs, and it only makes sense once deep snow has buried the brush. Parties commonly stash skis or boards around 2,500 ft in the old growth for the descent.
hazards: slide alder and slabs between roughly 1,100 and 2,200 ft when snow cover is thin
avalanche hazard in the gulch and on the glacier headwall in the early-season window
waysIn.whyThisWay: Early season with deep snow burying the slide alder, mostly for ski parties; it saves distance but is a steep bushwhack with overhead slide hazard in poor snow.

name: Standard Scramble
approach: Barlow Pass Trailhead (2,362 ft) → 4 miles on the gated Monte Cristo Road to the townsite (bike-friendly) → cross the South Fork Sauk River near mile 1 via a large log or ford (no bridge — flooding destroyed the old Twin Bridges) → Glacier Basin Trail #719 toward the basin (~4,400–4,680 ft) → leave trail and scramble to the dividing ridge and the summit. The final summit block is rated Class 4 (per the 1970 first-ascent record), not a pure walk-up — expect short, exposed scrambling moves near the top, and confirm you're on the correct ridge before committing, since parties from this trailhead often end up on the neighboring East Wilmans Spire (a separate roped climb) instead.
descent: Reverse the Class 3-4 scramble from the summit blocks down the ridge and slopes to Glacier Basin, watching for loose rock. From the basin, follow Glacier Basin Trail #719 down to the South Fork Sauk River crossing, then the gated Monte Cristo road about 4 miles back to Barlow Pass. A bicycle left at the gate saves time on the road.
hazards: Unbridged South Fork Sauk River crossing near mile 1 of the Monte Cristo road — log crossing or ford, riskier at high water
Loose, scree-covered talus on the approach gullies once snow melts out (worse by late summer) — rockfall hazard on the same slopes used by East Wilmans Spire climbers
Arsenic and heavy-metal contamination in surface water throughout the old Monte Cristo mining district — standard filtering/boiling will not remove it
Short Class 4 exposure on the final summit block per the historical first-ascent line
Remote off-trail routefinding above Glacier Basin; easy to end up on the wrong ridge feature (e.g., East Wilmans Spire) instead of the true summit

waysIn.name: Monte Cristo and Glacier Basin
waysIn.season: Midsummer to early autumn, once the basin talus is snow-free
waysIn.notes: From Barlow Pass walk the gated road to the old townsite; the road is bike-friendly and the river crossing near the first mile is a large log or a ford, with no bridge. Surface water near the townsite can carry arsenic and metals from old tailings, so treat or carry it. Past the townsite the Glacier Basin trail turns very steep and climbs wet, slick bedrock beside the falls — poor footing, worst on the descent — to the campsites on the timbered knoll where the maintained trail effectively ends. Leave the trail there and climb steep, very loose talus, or snow early in the season, to the col on the dividing ridge.
hazards: Slick wet bedrock beside the falls, especially descending
Steep, very loose talus gaining the col
A short exposed class 3-4 step on the summit block that is not a walk-up
Contaminated surface water near the old townsite

name: South Trail / Lookout Route
approach: From the Twin Lakes trailhead (elev. ~5,200ft, parking area between the two lakes, vault toilet on site), pick up Winchester Mountain Trail #685 heading north-northwest. The trail starts as a moderately steep, well-graded tread through blueberry and heather slopes. At about 0.25-0.5 mile you reach the signed junction with High Pass Trail #676 (which continues on toward Gargett Mine and Mt. Larrabee views) — stay left/straight to remain on #685 for Winchester. Beyond the junction the trail breaks out of the last scattered trees onto open, treeless southeast-facing slopes and climbs via a series of tight switchbacks through fireweed and heather, with steadily improving views back over Twin Lakes, Tomyhoi Peak, and Mt. Baker to the south. Around 0.9 mile there is an unmarked climbers'-path junction offering a more direct, rougher scramble line up snow/scree — the standard trail continues via switchbacks and is the preferred line for most parties. At roughly 1.3 miles the trail crests the ridge just west/south of the summit; from there it's a short final push of a few hundred feet of elevation along the open ridge to the summit and the 1935 fire lookout at 6,521ft. Total distance is about 3.4-3.5 miles round trip with 1,300-1,320ft of gain, so this leg (trailhead to summit) is roughly 1.7 miles and the full gain one-way. There is no reliable water on route or at the lookout — carry all you need. The main approach hazards are: the rough final 2.5 miles of FS-3065 to the trailhead (high-clearance recommended, 4WD helpful but not required, one-lane in places), and lingering steep snow on the upper switchbacks and southeast slopes that can persist into August in heavy-snow years — an ice axe and comfort with steep snow travel is recommended for early-season ascents, since a slip on the hardened snow above the switchbacks has real consequences given the exposure below.
descent: This is a walk-off, not a rappel route — descend by reversing the ascent trail (Winchester Mountain Trail #685) back down the switchbacks to the High Pass Trail #676 junction and on to the Twin Lakes trailhead. No rappels are involved. The only descent-specific caution is on the upper open switchbacks and the short ridge section just below the summit/lookout, where any lingering snow patches (common into July, occasionally into August) can be firm and exposed on the downhill side — plunge-step carefully or use an ice axe if the snow is present, since this is the same terrain flagged as the trail's main hazard on the way up. Below the switchbacks the trail is straightforward and well-graded back to the trailhead.
hazards: Steep, exposed snowfields on the slopes the trail traverses below the summit, lingering into July and sometimes August
Narrow, high-clearance-only final ~2.5 miles of FS Road 3065 with no guardrails and few pullouts
No water source at the lookout or along most of the trail
Black bear activity in the area — store food and scented items properly
Afternoon thunderstorms possible in summer on the exposed summit
Unmarked junction near 0.9 mile can cause route-finding confusion

waysIn.name: Winchester Mountain Trail #685 from Twin Lakes to the 1935 lookout
waysIn.season: Roughly Jul-Oct, and the limiting factor is the last two and a half miles of FS-3065 rather than the trail
waysIn.notes:
From the Twin Lakes trailhead at about 5,200 ft — the parking area between the two lakes, with a vault toilet — pick up Winchester Mountain Trail #685 heading north-northwest. It starts as a moderately steep, well-graded tread through blueberry and heather.

At roughly a quarter to half a mile there is a signed junction with High Pass Trail #676, which goes on toward the Gargett Mine and Mount Larrabee. Stay left or straight to remain on #685.

Beyond the junction the trail leaves the last trees onto open, treeless southeast-facing slopes and climbs by tight switchbacks. Around 0.9 mile an unmarked climbers' path splits off offering a more direct, rougher scramble line up snow and scree; the standard trail continues by switchbacks and is the preferred line.

At about 1.3 miles the trail crests the ridge just west and south of the summit; a short final push along the open ridge reaches the 1935 fire lookout at 6,521 ft. About 3.4-3.5 miles round trip with 1,300 ft of gain.

There is no water on route or at the lookout.
hazards: The last two and a half miles of FS-3065, rough and one-lane in places, high-clearance recommended
Hard lingering snow on the upper switchbacks into August in heavy-snow years, over consequential runout
A signed junction at 0.25-0.5 mile that serves five much larger objectives
An unmarked climbers' path at 0.9 mile up snow and scree
No water on route or at the lookout

name: Northeast Slabs
approach: Start at the Alpental Ski Area parking lot (~3,100 ft; I-90 Exit 52, north on Alpental Rd). Follow the Snow Lake Trail north into the valley on climber's-left of the outlet creek. In summer, stay on the maintained tread about 1.8-2 miles to the signed Source Lake Trail junction (~4,100 ft); in winter/spring the standard line leaves the summer trail earlier and climbs directly up the valley bottom/climbers'-path toward Source Lake — do not follow the exact summer boot path once there's meaningful snow cover, since it crosses avalanche terrain. From the Source Lake junction, leave the maintained trail and pick up the cairned climbers' path/talus traverse that runs above and around the east side of Source Lake, staying below the cliff band, aiming toward The Tooth's northeast aspect. Continue into the basin beneath the NE Face and ascend the broad snow finger/gully ("snow cone") that leads directly to the base of the Northeast Slabs route on the NE Face — cache skis in the hollow below and left of the route start before racking up. Figure roughly 2-2.5 miles and 1,500-2,000 ft of gain from the trailhead to the base of the climb; parties commonly do trailhead-to-summit-and-back in 4-6 hours in good firm-snow conditions. Hazards: this valley (Source Lake basin and the slopes below The Tooth) carries a well-documented history of avalanche accidents, rated "Challenging" avalanche terrain — assess stability seriously, especially in the transitional April-June snowpack the route is often climbed in, and do not treat the summer path as safe once snow is present. There are one or two creek crossings near the Source Lake outlet that can require removing skis or careful rock-hopping in high early-season flow. Above the talus the route-finding is cairned/boot-track only (no maintained tread), which can be tricky in whiteout or fresh snow.
descent: From the summit, downclimb a short distance to the tree anchor in the small notch just below the true summit. From there, rappel the South Face line to the notch (Pineapple Pass) between The Tooth and its south sub-summit — four rappels of under 30 m on a single 60 m rope, or two long ones with two 60 m ropes; parties often note the second rappel can pull stiffly, so flake the rope and check your pull direction before committing. Some parties instead rappel off a chockstone lower on the gully, but this is described as less efficient than the tree-anchor double rappel and is not the standard line. From the notch you join the South Face (standard) descent: downclimb/walk the gully and talus down through Great Scott Bowl, then retrace the approach traverse back above Source Lake to the Snow Lake/Source Lake trail and the Alpental lot. In good winter/spring coverage this whole descent from the notch is frequently skied or glissaded — parties report as little as ~10 minutes from the notch back to the car on skis in prime conditions; on foot through talus, plan on more like 45-60 minutes. The same avalanche exposure noted on the approach applies to the descent, and expect possible traffic from parties climbing the South Face route if your lines overlap near Pineapple Pass.
hazards: Crux Pitch 2 is an essentially unprotectable ~30m horizontal traverse on 50-60° snow/ice — serious fall consequences if it goes
Avalanche terrain on the Source Lake approach and the snow cone below the route
Conditions swing widely year to year — can range from solid neve to bare rock and verglas
Possible cornices near the summit ridge in heavy-snow years
Short winter daylight hours

waysIn.name: Alpental valley to the northeast basin (winter)
waysIn.season: Dec-Mar, and into spring on firm snow
waysIn.notes: From the Alpental upper lot (about 3,100 ft), go up the valley on the left side of the creek toward Source Lake, following the Source Lake line and whatever ski or boot track exists. In winter this means the valley bottom rather than the summer switchbacks, which cross the valley's avalanche chutes. Beyond Source Lake, climb the snow finger into the basin on the Tooth's northeast side, then continue up the snow slope beneath the face. Skis are normally cached at the bottom of that slope. Route-finding above the talus is cairn and boot-track only — there is no maintained tread — so fresh snow or a whiteout removes the only navigational aid you have.
hazards: Source Lake basin and the slopes below the Tooth have a documented avalanche accident history and are rated challenging avalanche terrain
the summer path is not a safe line once snow is present
thin, poorly protectable ice on the second pitch with long runouts
creek crossings near the Source Lake outlet at high flow
no maintained tread above the talus - navigation is by cairn and boot track only

name: South Face / Standard Route
approach: From the Stuart Lake Trailhead (Mountaineer Creek Trail #1599, elev. ~3,400 ft; Northwest Forest Pass required) at the end of Icicle Creek/Eightmile Road (FR 7601), follow the trail steadily uphill through forest along Mountaineer Creek. At about 2.5 miles, bear left at the signed junction onto the Colchuck Lake Trail (the right fork continues to Lake Stuart). Continue climbing, crossing a boulder-strewn section near the outlet, to reach Colchuck Lake (5,570 ft) at roughly mile 4, having gained about 2,000-2,100 ft — this is the last reliable water source before Aasgard Pass. Pick up the rough climbers' path along the lake's west shore (boulder-hopping in places) to its south end, then begin the well-known Aasgard Pass climb: an unrelenting, loose boot-track/goat-trail ascent of roughly 2,200 ft in under a mile to the 7,750-7,800 ft pass. This is the crux of the approach — footing is loose scree and talus lower down, the gully sections can be wet or icy, and snow commonly lingers into July, making an ice axe (and sometimes crampons/self-arrest practice) advisable; it is also a well-documented spot for slips given the sustained steepness and long runout. From the pass, work south to southwest across talus (and often a residual snow patch) toward the base of Dragontail Peak's east side, passing the west shore of Brynhild Lake and swinging around behind Witches Tower's distinctive summit spire to its south base — the pinnacle that divides the upper Snow Creek Glacier basin between Little Annapurna and Dragontail. All told, trailhead to the base of the tower is on the order of 6.5-7 miles one-way with roughly 4,700-4,900 ft of gain (consistent with the ~14-mile, ~5,400 ft round-trip car-to-car days reported by parties who do this as a single push). There is significant exposure on the ledge traverse near the top, and the Enchantments are prone to fast-building afternoon thunderstorms in summer, so an early start is standard practice.
descent: Descend by reversing the scramble: back across the four-foot summit slot, down the large blocks, and around the exposed ledge to the south base of the tower. The ledge is the part to take slowly, especially if it is wet or holds snow. From the base, retrace the approach past Brynhild Lake to Aasgard Pass, then down the loose 2,200 ft gully to Colchuck Lake (plunge-step or glissade any snow with an ice axe in hand) and out on the Colchuck Lake and Stuart Lake trails to the trailhead. No rappels are needed.
hazards: Loose, blocky rock and occasional rockfall on the approach ledges and scramble sections
Significant exposure on the unroped ledge traverse and the summit blocks
Snow and ice lingering on Aasgard Pass and the approach into July, requiring an ice axe (crampons in early season)
Afternoon thunderstorms are common July-August — start early and be off the summit by early afternoon
No reliable water source between Colchuck Lake and the summit

waysIn.name: Aasgard Pass, then past Brynhild Lake and around to the south side of the tower
waysIn.season: Roughly Jul-Sep; earlier the traverse from the pass is a snow crossing and the slopes below the tower want an axe
waysIn.notes:
From the Stuart Lake trailhead at about 3,400 ft, follow the Stuart Lake Trail south along Mountaineer Creek; at about 2.5 miles bear left at the signed junction onto the Colchuck Lake Trail. Cross Mountaineer Creek on logs and boulders — an awkward wet ford in early-season high water — and climb through forest and a boulder field to Colchuck Lake at 5,570 ft, roughly four miles in. Last reliable water.

Take the climbers' path along the lake's west shore through talus to the foot of Aasgard Pass, then up the eroded boot track: roughly 2,200 ft in well under a mile of loose scree and blocks, holding snow and ice into July.

From the pass at about 7,800 ft, work south to southwest across talus — initially as though heading for the snow route on Dragontail's east side — toward the tower, then up beside the west shore of Brynhild Lake (snow early in the season) and around behind the tower to its south base.

Figure six and a half to seven miles one way with something like 4,700-4,900 ft of gain.
hazards: Aasgard Pass: 2,200 ft of loose eroded scree with rockfall from parties above, holding snow into July
Serious exposure on the ledge traverse onto the east side of the tower
A four-foot slot that must be jumped to reach the true summit, with real consequence
Fast-building afternoon thunderstorms with no shelter in the Upper Enchantments
The downclimb off the south face is the crux for most parties

name: Southwest Corner
approach: Same approach as the South Face route to Aasgard Pass (7,841 ft), then hike south toward the tower and ascend snow or Class 2 rock to the col just southwest of the peak (roughly 6-8 hours and about 4,800 ft of gain from the trailhead).
descent: From the summit, downclimb the south face (Class 2-3) back to the col SW of the tower, then descend to Aasgard Pass and back down the loose talus/scree (or snow) to Colchuck Lake and the trailhead - roughly 1 hour from summit to the col.
hazards: Loose rock on the ridge and face.
Snow/ice at the col even in summer, requiring axe/crampons for camp access.

waysIn.name: Aasgard Pass to the col southwest of the tower
waysIn.season: Roughly Jul-Sep
waysIn.notes:
Stuart Lake trailhead to Colchuck Lake at 5,570 ft, the boot path along the lake's west shore, Aasgard Pass at about 7,800 ft, then south across talus toward the tower and up snow or Class 2 rock to the col just southwest of it.

Published figures for the day put it at roughly six to eight hours and about 4,800 ft of gain from the trailhead to this point, which is a wide enough spread that it should be treated as a range rather than a plan.

From the col the climbing is short: about 100 ft up the sharp ridge, a few feet right onto the south face at Class 4, a 5.5 step-up, a short face, and a scramble to the summit slot.
hazards: Aasgard Pass: loose steep scree, snow into July
Exposure on the sharp ridge above the col
Hard-to-find protection on the 5.5 crux
A four-foot summit slot that must be jumped
Afternoon thunderstorms with no shelter
Downclimbing the south face back to the col is the usual descent and is Class 2-3 with one harder step

name: West Buttress
approach: Same approach as the other routes: Stuart Lake/Colchuck Lake Trailhead to Colchuck Lake (5,570 ft), then the steep Aasgard Pass trail to the col behind Witches Tower; a steep snowfield crossing (ice axe recommended) leads to the route's base on the west side.
descent: Descend via a combination of rappelling and downclimbing, including a notably exposed ledge traverse, back to the col/notch; from there, downclimb the steep snowfield (self-arrest position with ice axe) back toward Aasgard Pass and out via Colchuck Lake to the trailhead.
hazards: Loose gendarmes/blocks in places.
Steep snow on the approach that can be firm/icy early or late season.

waysIn.name: Aasgard Pass to the col, then a steep snowfield crossing onto the west side
waysIn.season: Roughly Jul-Sep. The snowfield is the point of this variant and it is present through most of the usable season — carry an axe regardless of the date
waysIn.notes:
As for the other routes on the tower: Stuart Lake trailhead, the Colchuck Lake Trail to Colchuck Lake at 5,570 ft, the boot path round the lake, and Aasgard Pass at about 7,800 ft. Then south across the basin to the col behind the tower.

What is different here is the last few hundred feet. From the col a steep snowfield has to be crossed to reach the base of the buttress on the west side. An ice axe is the standard recommendation, and parties downclimb it in self-arrest position on the way out, which tells you the angle.

The climbing above is mostly Class 4 on solid granite with good holds, a short Class 5 chimney partway up, and a friction section to finish. Two pitches.

The descent combines rappelling and downclimbing, including an exposed ledge traverse, back to the col — so the snowfield gets crossed twice.
hazards: A steep snowfield crossing to reach the base, and again in descent — ice axe essential
Aasgard Pass: loose steep scree, snow into July
An exposed ledge traverse on the descent
A short Class 5 chimney mid-route with a pack
Afternoon thunderstorms with no shelter and a snow crossing between you and the way out

name: Standard Scramble
approach: Park at the Thirtymile Trailhead (~3,400 ft) at the end of West Chewuch Road, about 29 miles north of Winthrop. From there follow the Chewuch River Trail #510 north, staying close to the Chewuch River; Chewuch Falls is a good landmark around 2.5 miles in. Around mile 8 to 8.8 the trail crosses a 2001 burn area — standing dead snags are common here and more prone to falling in wind, so be alert in storms. At roughly 8-8.8 miles (~4,700 ft) reach the signed junction with Tungsten Creek Trail #534, just after fording Horseshoe Creek, and turn right onto it. Follow Tungsten Creek Trail #534 for 6.2 miles, gaining about 2,100 ft, passing within earshot of Big Horn and Horseshoe Creeks and crossing Cinch Creek; Tungsten Creek itself, which the trail follows for its final stretch, is the last dependable water before the high country (in dry years, e.g. a September 2017 trip, sources beyond here were reported as dry streambeds and stagnant pools, so tank up). This trail ends at its junction with the Boundary Trail #533 at the historic Tungsten Mine Camp (~6,750 ft) — old mine structures, iron pipe, and building ruins from the 1908-1920s tungsten operation are visible on the south side of Wolframite Mountain. This point is roughly 14-15 miles in, effectively a full day's hike, and most parties camp near here rather than pushing to the summit and back in one day. From the mine camp junction, follow the Boundary Trail #533 west for about 1 mile to the point where the trail bends south toward Apex Pass. Leave the trail here and ascend off-trail, heading northeast up Wolframite's broad, gentle west slopes to the 8,136-8,137 ft summit; done on this line the terrain is a straightforward Class 2 talus/heather slope, though other lines or variations can involve short sections of low Class 3. This is the safest and most recommended line up the peak. Total one-way distance from the trailhead is roughly 16-17 miles with about 4,700 ft of cumulative gain, consistent with the ~34-mile (54.72 km) round trip — treat this as a backpack with a high camp near Tungsten Mine or the Boundary Trail, not a single-day car-to-car scramble. In mid-October the first 8.8 miles on the river trail are flat with few fallen trees, and the wide creek ford at the horse camp can be crossed on rocks.
descent: This is a walk-off with no rappelling required (rappels: 0). The standard and recommended descent reverses the ascent line: down Wolframite's west slopes (Class 2 talus/heather, with loose rock and scree underfoot — stay grouped and avoid kicking rock onto anyone below) back to the Boundary Trail #533 where it bends near Apex Pass, then east on the Boundary Trail back to the Tungsten Mine Camp junction, and finally back out via Tungsten Creek Trail #534 and the Chewuch River Trail #510 to the Thirtymile Trailhead. Parties linking Wolframite with neighboring peaks (Barchester Towers, The Pope) have also used an alternate cross-country descent off the north side: down into Wolframite's northeast basin, crossing just below a talus field, then climbing to a roughly 7,000 ft col before bushwhacking down to intersect the Boundary Trail. That variant is rougher and brushier and only makes sense as part of a multi-peak traverse; for a straightforward out-and-back, reversing the west-slope ascent route is the way to go. No fixed anchors, bolts, or technical rope work exist anywhere on this route.
hazards: Extremely long, remote wilderness approach with no cell coverage — a serious injury or illness far in means a multi-day self-extraction or rescue
Early/late-season snow squalls above 7,000 ft can arrive with little warning, even in early-mid October per a documented trip report
Tungsten Creek and Chewuch River fords can be higher and more difficult in early season/high snowmelt
Off-trail Class 2-3 talus and scree on the summit slopes require basic route-finding
Black bear, cougar, and reported wolf activity along the Chewuch/Boundary Trail corridor; area lies within the North Cascades grizzly bear recovery zone
Unstable historic mine debris/equipment near the Tungsten Mine Camp site

waysIn.name: Boundary Trail from Tungsten Mine Camp
waysIn.season: July to September
waysIn.notes: The scramble here is trivial and the approach is not, so treat this as a multi-day backpack with a short walk-up at the end of it. From the road end at Thirtymile the Chewuch River trail runs north for eight or nine miles, passing a waterfall a couple of miles in and crossing a burn where standing snags are a real concern in wind, to a signed junction where the Tungsten Creek trail turns off. That trail climbs a further six miles and about two thousand feet to the old mine camp on the mountain's south side, where the Boundary Trail comes in. The creek the trail follows on its last stretch is the final dependable water; in dry years everything above it can be dry streambed and stagnant pools. Most parties camp near the mine and climb the peak the following morning.
hazards: Extremely long remote approach with no cell coverage
Early or late season snow squalls above 7,000 ft arriving with little warning
Higher, more difficult fords of Tungsten Creek and the Chewuch in early season
Standing fire-killed snags through the burned section in wind
Unstable historic mine debris and equipment near the camp
Loose talus and scree on the summit slopes
Bear, cougar and wolf country - proper food storage required
